Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday, November 12, following the exposure of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct subordinate, is already discussing a plan to return to the company with his confidants. This was reported on Sunday, November 15, by the British newspaper Financial Times. According to an associate of the businessman, Silicon Valley top executives have formed a dedicated "war room" to lobby Nvidia's board of directors for Huang's reinstatement, as well as to try to secure support in the White House. "Everyone who matters in tech outside of the frontier labs loves Jensen," said an interlocutor of the publication, adding that these efforts have the backing of the former CEO himself. Over the weekend, the public campaign for the return of the founder of the $4 trillion corporation gained momentum. Back on Friday, major shareholders of the company—Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management head Gavin Baker—published an appeal to the corporate leadership, urging them to keep "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang," given his decades of service and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the business. Despite pressure from billionaires and investors, the push to rehabilitate Huang faces severe legal and political obstacles. Unlike many other tech titan founders, Huang does not hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and therefore cannot veto decisions made by the board of directors. The board itself is currently conducting an independent investigation into the former chief's conduct. Even those in the businessman's camp acknowledge the weakness of his position. "An affair with a subordinate is a firing offense," admitted one member of Huang's support group. Aside from the internal workplace affair with Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell, Huang's primary problem stems from his connection to Alice Huang, head of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which US authorities suspect of espionage and smuggling chips into China. This episode has drawn intense scrutiny toward how Nvidia monitors the sales of its artificial intelligence processors to clients in Asia. On Sunday, November 15, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly called for a "radical refresh" in Nvidia's leadership following the departure of its founder. Meanwhile, the corporation's interim CEO Colette Kress is preparing the company for the release of its quarterly financial report on Tuesday, while the board of directors is already looking for a permanent successor. According to the Financial Times, Nvidia representatives have approached Rene Haas, CEO of the British processor architecture designer Arm Holdings, with an offer to head the corporation, though officially the company states that a formal process to select a new leader has not yet been launched. Representatives of Nvidia and Jensen Huang himself declined to comment on his potential return.

extraction.body: Just three days after the high-profile resignation of the founder of the world's most valuable chipmaker, his supporters in Silicon Valley have set up a dedicated war room to pressure the board of directors. However, regaining the seat will not be easy for the billionaire: he does not hold a controlling stake, while the corporation is already scouting for his replacement and bracing for scrutiny from Washington. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday, November 12, following the exposure of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct subordinate, is already discussing a plan to return to the company with his confidants. This was reported on Sunday, November 15, by the British newspaper Financial Times. According to an associate of the businessman, Silicon Valley top executives have formed a dedicated "war room" to lobby Nvidia's board of directors for Huang's reinstatement, as well as to try to secure support in the White House. "Everyone who matters in tech outside of the frontier labs loves Jensen," said an interlocutor of the publication, adding that these efforts have the backing of the former CEO himself. Over the weekend, the public campaign for the return of the founder of the $4 trillion corporation gained momentum. An open letter to the board of directors demanding to "Bring Jensen Back" was supported by Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as several Nvidia employees. Back on Friday, major shareholders of the company—Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management head Gavin Baker—published an appeal to the corporate leadership, urging them to keep "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang," given his decades of service and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the business. Despite pressure from billionaires and investors, the push to rehabilitate Huang faces severe legal and political obstacles. Unlike many other tech titan founders, Huang does not hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and therefore cannot veto decisions made by the board of directors. sources.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
passages: China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing.

On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.

Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing .
Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised.
There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Jensen Huang discusses comeback as Nvidia CEO with allies: report
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

extraction.body: [BEIJING] Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s artificial intelligence data centre market, but a Reuters review has identified more than US$3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors. The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom . The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan (US$3.2 billion). The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion. They reveal the company’s technology reaches well beyond China’s largest tech firms, into local government-backed ventures, universities and regional computing centres. The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations. It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone. China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment. The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing . Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero. The company has also excluded China data centre computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty. That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement. “Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power – and for what purpose,” said Cheung. Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors. These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived. While some facilities are already operational or under construction, operators are exposed to potential delays, supply disruptions, or costly redesigns around domestic chips as export controls tighten. Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls. Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800. In January, the Trump administration moved to review H200 export licences for eligible Chinese customers individually , subject to conditions. Nvidia’s August filing said it was effectively excluded from China’s data centre computing market. The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .

The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan (US$3.2 billion).
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
They reveal the company’s technology reaches well beyond China’s largest tech firms, into local government-backed ventures, universities and regional computing centres.

The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations. It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing .
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.
The company has also excluded China data centre computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty.

That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors.
Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement.
“Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power – and for what purpose,” said Cheung.
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.

While some facilities are already operational or under construction, operators are exposed to potential delays, supply disruptions, or costly redesigns around domestic chips as export controls tighten.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.

Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang's departure from NVIDIA has sparked varied reactions across Asia, with some governments confirming their commitment to chip supplies and others assessing the impact on local projects or ongoing investigations. The move comes after reports of a Chinese spy operation targeting Huang and his admission of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. China's foreign ministry has denied allegations that a Chinese businesswoman linked to Huang was a spy, calling them baseless and an attempt to defame Beijing. The ministry also opposed export controls disrupting global supply chains and denied knowledge of reports connecting restricted NVIDIA chips with a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang. However, Huang's exit has raised concerns over more than $3 billion worth of Chinese AI computing projects dependent on NVIDIA's restricted processors. In Singapore, authorities seized Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed's passport in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases. The probe looked into whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. While police found insufficient evidence to prove offenses related to false declarations in February 2026, they said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. South Korea's Science Ministry said NVIDIA had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Meanwhile, Taiwan's Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang's departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry. Taipei's city government also confirmed that NVIDIA's planned overseas headquarters in Taipei remains on track despite this leadership change. Japan's Industry Ministry has said it will closely monitor NVIDIA after Huang's resignation, considering the chipmaker a key player in Japan's AI semiconductor industry. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it's too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry but emphasized Japan's commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

coreStoryFacts.text: Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.

The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports.
H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.
Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.
Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information.
Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.

Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. extraction.body: [BEIJING] Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s artificial intelligence data centre market, but a Reuters review has identified more than US$3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors. The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom . The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan (US$3.2 billion). The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion. They reveal the company’s technology reaches well beyond China’s largest tech firms, into local government-backed ventures, universities and regional computing centres. The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations. It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone. China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment. The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing . Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero. The company has also excluded China data centre computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty. That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement. “Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power – and for what purpose,” said Cheung. Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors. sources.title: How Asian governments responded to NVIDIA CEO's departure
passages: Jensen Huang's departure from NVIDIA has sparked varied reactions across Asia, with some governments confirming their commitment to chip supplies and others assessing the impact on local projects or ongoing investigations.
Taipei's city government also confirmed that NVIDIA's planned overseas headquarters in Taipei remains on track despite this leadership change.
However, Huang's exit has raised concerns over more than $3 billion worth of Chinese AI computing projects dependent on NVIDIA's restricted processors.
The ministry also opposed export controls disrupting global supply chains and denied knowledge of reports connecting restricted NVIDIA chips with a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang.
Japan's Industry Ministry has said it will closely monitor NVIDIA after Huang's resignation, considering the chipmaker a key player in Japan's AI semiconductor industry.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang's departure from NVIDIA has sparked varied reactions across Asia, with some governments confirming their commitment to chip supplies and others assessing the impact on local projects or ongoing investigations. The move comes after reports of a Chinese spy operation targeting Huang and his admission of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. China's foreign ministry has denied allegations that a Chinese businesswoman linked to Huang was a spy, calling them baseless and an attempt to defame Beijing. The ministry also opposed export controls disrupting global supply chains and denied knowledge of reports connecting restricted NVIDIA chips with a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang. However, Huang's exit has raised concerns over more than $3 billion worth of Chinese AI computing projects dependent on NVIDIA's restricted processors. In Singapore, authorities seized Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed's passport in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases. The probe looked into whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. While police found insufficient evidence to prove offenses related to false declarations in February 2026, they said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. South Korea's Science Ministry said NVIDIA had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Meanwhile, Taiwan's Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang's departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry. Taipei's city government also confirmed that NVIDIA's planned overseas headquarters in Taipei remains on track despite this leadership change. Japan's Industry Ministry has said it will closely monitor NVIDIA after Huang's resignation, considering the chipmaker a key player in Japan's AI semiconductor industry. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it's too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry but emphasized Japan's commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

Strategy says it will keep STRC's 12% rate until the stock trades steadily near $100. STRC climbed back to $100 earlier this month, and buybacks help hold it there.

Strive spent $17.5 million, about half of Strategy's outlay, while holding roughly 5% as much Bitcoin.

Its reserve and USD Cash balances stood at $4.75 billion and $151.2 million, respectively, on Nov. 15. Strategy also maintained STRC’s annual dividend rate at 12% for December, declaring daily dividends totaling $1 per share for the month. Strategy’s Bitcoin treasury has accumulated approximately $9.8 billion in unrealized losses as the crypto market sell-off deepened, according to tracker data. The downturn follows a volatile week for the crypto market, during which MSCI decided to remove the company from its global indexes. Strategy stock fell approximately 8.5% to $111.60 from $122 after the announcement, then lost another 8.5% in early Monday trading. Bitcoin dropped to $62,000 over the weekend after failing to sustain prices above $69,000 and traded near $64,200 at press time, marking a 14% decline over seven days. Strategy CEO Phong Le said MSCI’s decision would have a limited effect, with approximately 3% of Strategy shares tied to the index provider’s benchmarks. Le called the exclusion “immaterial,” arguing that index providers should serve as independent arbiters rather than choose which investments are appropriate for market participants.

extraction.body: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here . Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. passages: SpaceX Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder were among more than 158,000 signatories by Sunday demanding Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief pending an independent investigation.

Huang resigned Thursday after revelations of two extramarital affairs, one with a subordinate and another with a woman accused of spying for China, ending his 33-year tenure at the helm of the artificial intelligence giant.

extraction.body: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) had enough to deal with on Wednesday night. The Wall Street Journal reported at 5:27 PM ET that its board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang and could meet as soon as Wednesday, hours after a New York Times report that Huang had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has not commented. The same day, its biggest customer laid out a long-term plan that runs through Nvidia’s profit margin. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told about 50 presidents of Samsung companies that OpenAI’s edge will come from owning the whole stack. Asked whether heavy spending was squeezing returns, Altman said “that’s the point”: a company with “vertically integrated infrastructure that costs less than any other company’s” can sell AI in huge volume at thin margins and pull ahead of the competition, according to Q&A materials from the October 31 meeting obtained by Korea’s Financial News and published Wednesday. The article says OpenAI’s investments in efficiency, including chips it designs itself, are starting to pay off. Read plainly, that is a plan to stop paying Nvidia’s prices. Nvidia sells the most expensive layer of AI infrastructure at some of the widest margins in the industry. A customer whose strategy is to run that infrastructure cheaper than anyone else has to replace that layer with its own over the medium to long term. Nvidia was at $160.03 in after-hours trading at 7:15 PM ET, down 7.9% from Wednesday’s close, 14.3% below the November 6 close and 33.1% below its October 6 record close. OpenAI has been building toward this for a year. In 2025 it signed a letter of intent with Nvidia for 10 gigawatts of Nvidia systems, with Nvidia planning to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as they were deployed. Within weeks it agreed to buy 6 gigawatts of AMD chips and announced a 10-gigawatt deal with Broadcom to build custom accelerators of OpenAI’s own design, with deployment starting in the second half of 2026. Each step moves more of OpenAI’s computing away from a single supplier, and the Broadcom chips move it onto silicon OpenAI controls. Altman’s remarks to Samsung explain why. Selling AI in high volumes at thin margins only works if the cost of each unit of computing keeps falling, and the fastest way to cut that cost is to stop paying a supplier’s markup. “If we can build vertically integrated infrastructure at a lower cost than anyone else,” as one English translation of his comment circulating on X put it, “we can get ahead of the competition.” Altman made two other points in the same meeting that Nvidia holders will not like. He said “there has been double-counting of demand” for AI, and that “only two companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are actually driving major demand growth.” A boom that rests on two buyers gives those two buyers enormous bargaining power, and one of them has just described a plan to need Nvidia less. He also gave the bull case: “In the long term, AI demand will grow enormously,” and the biggest limit for the next few years is “the chip supply chain and data center infrastructure.” The world is still short of chips, which keeps Nvidia’s sales high for now. The question for a holder is what Nvidia can charge once its largest customers make their own. A holder who had $100,000 in Nvidia at the November 6 close, about 536 shares, has about $85,743 at the after-hours price, a loss of about $14,257 in three trading sessions and an evening. Almost all of that came from the Huang scandal. Altman’s plan is a slower risk: it goes to Nvidia’s gross margin, the number to watch in every quarterly report from here, and it matters more over five years than who is CEO next month. For a holder deciding what to do before Thursday’s open, the practical question is concentration. If Nvidia is more than about 10% of a retirement portfolio, both the board’s decision and OpenAI’s plan land on that one position. Trimming inside an IRA costs nothing in taxes. Trimming in a taxable account turns part of the gain into a tax bill, which is worth knowing before selling on a night like this. Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections. Selling AI in high volumes at thin margins only works if the cost of each unit of computing keeps falling, and the fastest way to cut that cost is to stop paying a supplier’s markup. “If we can build vertically integrated infrastructure at a lower cost than anyone else,” as one English translation of his comment circulating on X put it, “we can get ahead of the competition.”

Altman made two other points in the same meeting that Nvidia holders will not like. He said “there has been double-counting of demand” for AI, and that “only two companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are actually driving major demand growth.” A boom that rests on two buyers gives those two buyers enormous bargaining power, and one of them has just described a plan to need Nvidia less.

He also gave the bull case: “In the long term, AI demand will grow enormously,” and the biggest limit for the next few years is “the chip supply chain and data center infrastructure.” The world is still short of chips, which keeps Nvidia’s sales high for now. The question for a holder is what Nvidia can charge once its largest customers make their own.

A holder who had $100,000 in Nvidia at the November 6 close, about 536 shares, has about $85,743 at the after-hours price, a loss of about $14,257 in three trading sessions and an evening. Almost all of that came from the Huang scandal. Altman’s plan is a slower risk: it goes to Nvidia’s gross margin, the number to watch in every quarterly report from here, and it matters more over five years than who is CEO next month.

For a holder deciding what to do before Thursday’s open, the practical question is concentration. If Nvidia is more than about 10% of a retirement portfolio, both the board’s decision and OpenAI’s plan land on that one position. Trimming inside an IRA costs nothing in taxes. Trimming in a taxable account turns part of the gain into a tax bill, which is worth knowing before selling on a night like this.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back with another 'China warning' for the United States of America. In a recent appearance on Dwarkesh Podcast, Huang once again said that working with China then 'against China' is in the interests of the US. He said that the migration from Nvidia’s CUDA to Huawei’s CANN framework threatens to break the software-hardware dependency underpinning American AI dominance, even as US lawmakers push to place DeepSeek on the entity list for export control.Nvidia CEO said, "We have got to acknowledge that most of the advances in AI came out of algorithm advances, not just the raw hardware. The day that DeepSeek comes out on Huawei first, that is a horrible outcome for our nation."When asked about how DeepSeek's being an open source model can hurt America's proprietary systems, considering that it can run on any system. You described a situation that I perceive to be good news. A company developed software, developed an AI model, and it runs best on the American tech stack. You set it up as a premise that it was bad news. I’m going to give you the bad news, that AI models around the world are developed and they run best on non-American hardware. That is bad news for us." When asked how shipping chips to China is keeping the US ahead, considering that the bottleneck is on compute. Number one, why is it that we don’t come up with a regulation that’s more balanced so that Nvidia can win around the world instead of giving up the world? Why would you want the United States to give up the world? The chip industry is part of the American ecosystem. Why is it that your policy, your philosophy, leads to the United States giving up a vast part of the world’s market?""United States is not a loser"Nvidia CEO sounded a bit upset when stressed on how America giving permission to Nvidia to sell its chips in China helps in the country's AI dominance. Huang replied after constant prodding, "We have to keep innovating and, as you probably know, our share is growing, not decreasing. The premise that even if we compete in China, that we’re going to lose that market anyways… You’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser. The fact that I can buy this car brand one day and use another car brand another day, easy. Because I don’t think the United States is a loser.

extraction.body: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here . Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly. But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more. Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind. I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America. I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him. Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang. Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair. Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups. People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions. Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this? Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie. Where was Nvidia’s security team? extraction.body: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) had enough to deal with on Wednesday night. The Wall Street Journal reported at 5:27 PM ET that its board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang and could meet as soon as Wednesday, hours after a New York Times report that Huang had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has not commented. The same day, its biggest customer laid out a long-term plan that runs through Nvidia’s profit margin. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told about 50 presidents of Samsung companies that OpenAI’s edge will come from owning the whole stack. Asked whether heavy spending was squeezing returns, Altman said “that’s the point”: a company with “vertically integrated infrastructure that costs less than any other company’s” can sell AI in huge volume at thin margins and pull ahead of the competition, according to Q&A materials from the October 31 meeting obtained by Korea’s Financial News and published Wednesday. The article says OpenAI’s investments in efficiency, including chips it designs itself, are starting to pay off. Read plainly, that is a plan to stop paying Nvidia’s prices. Nvidia sells the most expensive layer of AI infrastructure at some of the widest margins in the industry. A customer whose strategy is to run that infrastructure cheaper than anyone else has to replace that layer with its own over the medium to long term. Nvidia was at $160.03 in after-hours trading at 7:15 PM ET, down 7.9% from Wednesday’s close, 14.3% below the November 6 close and 33.1% below its October 6 record close. extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back with another 'China warning' for the United States of America. In a recent appearance on Dwarkesh Podcast, Huang once again said that working with China then 'against China' is in the interests of the US. He said that the migration from Nvidia’s CUDA to Huawei’s CANN framework threatens to break the software-hardware dependency underpinning American AI dominance, even as US lawmakers push to place DeepSeek on the entity list for export control.Nvidia CEO said, "We have got to acknowledge that most of the advances in AI came out of algorithm advances, not just the raw hardware. The day that DeepSeek comes out on Huawei first, that is a horrible outcome for our nation."When asked about how DeepSeek's being an open source model can hurt America's proprietary systems, considering that it can run on any system. You described a situation that I perceive to be good news. A company developed software, developed an AI model, and it runs best on the American tech stack. You set it up as a premise that it was bad news. I’m going to give you the bad news, that AI models around the world are developed and they run best on non-American hardware. That is bad news for us." When asked how shipping chips to China is keeping the US ahead, considering that the bottleneck is on compute. Number one, why is it that we don’t come up with a regulation that’s more balanced so that Nvidia can win around the world instead of giving up the world? Why would you want the United States to give up the world? The chip industry is part of the American ecosystem. Why is it that your policy, your philosophy, leads to the United States giving up a vast part of the world’s market?""United States is not a loser"Nvidia CEO sounded a bit upset when stressed on how America giving permission to Nvidia to sell its chips in China helps in the country's AI dominance. Huang replied after constant prodding, "We have to keep innovating and, as you probably know, our share is growing, not decreasing. The premise that even if we compete in China, that we’re going to lose that market anyways… You’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser. The fact that I can buy this car brand one day and use another car brand another day, easy. Because I don’t think the United States is a loser.

extraction.body: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months. The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week . passages: Apple and clinical AI platform OpenEvidence want up to 200,000 US participants to ask health questions and grade the answers
Sun 15 Nov 2026 · 20:30 EST · 3 min read
Apple wants to know whether AI health answers are actually any good. Rather than guess, it is asking up to 200,000 people to grade them.

The company announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, 2026, in partnership with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform built for healthcare professionals. Participants will use a dedicated iOS app to ask medical questions, then score the responses on accuracy, detail and relevance.
The study is virtual and limited to the US. Eligible participants must be 21 or older, and enrollment opened the same day as the announcement, with the app already available to download.

Once inside the app, users type in health questions the way they might ask a friend who went to medical school. The answers come from OpenEvidence, which grounds its responses in peer-reviewed literature, including The New England Journal of Medicine , JAMA and Nature.
After each answer, participants rate what they received. The research focuses on four areas: user trust, response quality, comprehension, and the effect on health decision-making.
Participants control their survey responses, and privacy protections apply throughout the study.

The study departs from Apple’s earlier health research, which centered on data collected by its devices. The Apple Health Study, which began in February 2025, is one example of that device-first approach.

OpenEvidence may not be a household name, but it has become a fixture in many clinicians’ workflows. Its user base among monthly active US clinicians grew from 355 in January 2024 to 703,265 by June 2026.
The platform has also handled 271 million queries over 30 months.
OpenEvidence reached a valuation of approximately $15 billion after a $250 million funding round in September 2026.
The company has also integrated with major US health systems, pushing clinical AI deeper into everyday hospital operations.
The launch comes as scrutiny of AI in healthcare intensifies. In mid-October 2026, JAMA published a comprehensive analysis of how clinicians use these tools, adding fuel to an already active debate.

For Apple, the study offers something valuable: large-scale, structured feedback on how people engage with health AI before committing to a consumer product. With up to 200,000 participants, the dataset could give the company a clearer picture of where these tools earn trust and where they lose it.
The stated goal is to improve conversational health AI design for Apple and for the wider healthcare industry.
The study’s focus on comprehension suggests both companies are aware that translating medical literature for laypeople without distorting it is a hard design problem.

extraction.body: Apple and clinical AI platform OpenEvidence want up to 200,000 US participants to ask health questions and grade the answers Sun 15 Nov 2026 · 20:30 EST · 3 min read Apple wants to know whether AI health answers are actually any good. Rather than guess, it is asking up to 200,000 people to grade them. The company announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, 2026, in partnership with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform built for healthcare professionals. Participants will use a dedicated iOS app to ask medical questions, then score the responses on accuracy, detail and relevance. The study is virtual and limited to the US. Eligible participants must be 21 or older, and enrollment opened the same day as the announcement, with the app already available to download. Once inside the app, users type in health questions the way they might ask a friend who went to medical school. The answers come from OpenEvidence, which grounds its responses in peer-reviewed literature, including The New England Journal of Medicine , JAMA and Nature. After each answer, participants rate what they received. The research focuses on four areas: user trust, response quality, comprehension, and the effect on health decision-making. Participants control their survey responses, and privacy protections apply throughout the study. The study departs from Apple’s earlier health research, which centered on data collected by its devices. The Apple Health Study, which began in February 2025, is one example of that device-first approach. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime. OpenEvidence may not be a household name, but it has become a fixture in many clinicians’ workflows. Its user base among monthly active US clinicians grew from 355 in January 2024 to 703,265 by June 2026. The platform has also handled 271 million queries over 30 months. OpenEvidence reached a valuation of approximately $15 billion after a $250 million funding round in September 2026. The company has also integrated with major US health systems, pushing clinical AI deeper into everyday hospital operations. The launch comes as scrutiny of AI in healthcare intensifies. In mid-October 2026, JAMA published a comprehensive analysis of how clinicians use these tools, adding fuel to an already active debate. For Apple, the study offers something valuable: large-scale, structured feedback on how people engage with health AI before committing to a consumer product. With up to 200,000 participants, the dataset could give the company a clearer picture of where these tools earn trust and where they lose it. The stated goal is to improve conversational health AI design for Apple and for the wider healthcare industry. The study’s focus on comprehension suggests both companies are aware that translating medical literature for laypeople without distorting it is a hard design problem. Apple wants to know whether AI health answers are actually any good. Rather than guess, it is asking up to 200,000 people to grade them.

The company announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, 2026, in partnership with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform built for healthcare professionals. Participants will use a dedicated iOS app to ask medical questions, then score the responses on accuracy, detail and relevance.
The study is virtual and limited to the US. Eligible participants must be 21 or older, and enrollment opened the same day as the announcement, with the app already available to download.

Once inside the app, users type in health questions the way they might ask a friend who went to medical school. The answers come from OpenEvidence, which grounds its responses in peer-reviewed literature, including The New England Journal of Medicine , JAMA and Nature.
After each answer, participants rate what they received. The research focuses on four areas: user trust, response quality, comprehension, and the effect on health decision-making.
Participants control their survey responses, and privacy protections apply throughout the study.

The study departs from Apple’s earlier health research, which centered on data collected by its devices. The Apple Health Study, which began in February 2025, is one example of that device-first approach.

OpenEvidence may not be a household name, but it has become a fixture in many clinicians’ workflows. Its user base among monthly active US clinicians grew from 355 in January 2024 to 703,265 by June 2026.
The platform has also handled 271 million queries over 30 months.
OpenEvidence reached a valuation of approximately $15 billion after a $250 million funding round in September 2026.
The company has also integrated with major US health systems, pushing clinical AI deeper into everyday hospital operations.
The launch comes as scrutiny of AI in healthcare intensifies. In mid-October 2026, JAMA published a comprehensive analysis of how clinicians use these tools, adding fuel to an already active debate.

For Apple, the study offers something valuable: large-scale, structured feedback on how people engage with health AI before committing to a consumer product. With up to 200,000 participants, the dataset could give the company a clearer picture of where these tools earn trust and where they lose it.
The stated goal is to improve conversational health AI design for Apple and for the wider healthcare industry.
The study’s focus on comprehension suggests both companies are aware that translating medical literature for laypeople without distorting it is a hard design problem.

extraction.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's spy-sex scandal . But the Commerce Department is in charge "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's " Squawk Box ." The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed. Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported. Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room. Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room." But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s." "And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy. Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales. Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down." "The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" "I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said. The Commerce Department did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Bessent's remarks. Huang and Lutnick both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Thursday . Eichamer, the Commerce spokeswoman, told CNBC on Friday that Lutnick "has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions." Huang has separately been asked to sit for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 before the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs. The Republican chairmen of those panels have also asked Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to participate in a closed-door interview with them on Dec. 2. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., separately asked Jeff Kessler, Commerce's under secretary for industry and security, to appear before his committee on Dec. 3 for a hearing on "chip smuggling, adversary military use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations." sources.title: Senator slams Commerce Secretary for flow of Nvidia AI chips to China
passages: Washington Senator Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia’s AI chips away from China.

The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for Commerce Secretary.

While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a new initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals.

Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries.
The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

In a letter to Lutnick on Sunday, Cantwell said the DOC has “undermined America’s national security,” and that its failures “help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.” > “Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology.” In her letter, Cantwell specifically calls out instances when the DOC reportedly didn’t heed warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed’s access to AI chips, prior to allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a then-Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy. Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries. The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for Commerce Secretary. The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, accused the Commerce Department in a letter to Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday, Nov. 15, of failing to stop advanced U.S. AI chips from reaching China, CNBC and The Verge reported [1] [2] . "Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People's Republic of China (PRC)," she wrote, adding that "these failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI" [1] [2] . Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving them [1] . She sent the letter ahead of President Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Thursday, Nov. 19 [1] [2] . The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Monday [1] . According to The Verge, the letter says Commerce did not act on warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed's access to AI chips before reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive U.S. officials suspect of passing information to China [2] . Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 . Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last week that the Megaspeed blacklisting stalled because Commerce "has the pen" . Cantwell also criticized Commerce for letting Alibaba and ByteDance use Nvidia chips through overseas data centers and for extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain U.S. AI technology through subsidiaries, The Verge reported [2] . The New York Times reported on Nov. 15 that Lutnick pushed for narrower rules on overseas data centers serving Chinese customers . On conflicts, Cantwell said Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick led and his sons now control, held $1.2 billion of Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination [1] . She said the administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology" [1] . "America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," she wrote [1] . CNBC reported last week that Cantor held 1.81 million Nvidia shares worth $362 million at the end of June. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) has summoned Jensen Huang and Lutnick to testify in December, and Commerce spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said last week that Lutnick has agreed to appear [1] . Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have given Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller until Nov. 17 to confirm they have ordered Nvidia export records preserved [1] . Lawmakers in both parties are also moving toward tighter AI chip export rules . "The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America's most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries," Cantwell wrote in closing [2] . Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that the administration plans to name Nvidia and other U.S. AI companies "national champions" to help them expand overseas.
