extraction.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's spy-sex scandal . But the Commerce Department is in charge "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's " Squawk Box ." The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed. Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported. Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room. Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room." But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s." "And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy. Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales. Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down." "The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" "I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said. The Commerce Department did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Bessent's remarks. Huang and Lutnick both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Thursday . Eichamer, the Commerce spokeswoman, told CNBC on Friday that Lutnick "has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions." Huang has separately been asked to sit for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 before the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs. The Republican chairmen of those panels have also asked Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to participate in a closed-door interview with them on Dec. 2. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., separately asked Jeff Kessler, Commerce's under secretary for industry and security, to appear before his committee on Dec. 3 for a hearing on "chip smuggling, adversary military use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations." Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.

Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down."

"The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"
"I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said.
The Commerce Department did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
Huang and Lutnick both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Thursday .
Eichamer, the Commerce spokeswoman, told CNBC on Friday that Lutnick "has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions."
Huang has separately been asked to sit for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 before the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs.
The Republican chairmen of those panels have also asked Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to participate in a closed-door interview with them on Dec. 2.

House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., separately asked Jeff Kessler, Commerce's under secretary for industry and security, to appear before his committee on Dec. 3 for a hearing on "chip smuggling, adversary military use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations."

While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a new initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals.

Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries.
The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, accused the Commerce Department in a letter to Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday, Nov. 15, of failing to stop advanced U.S. AI chips from reaching China, CNBC and The Verge reported [1] [2] . "Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People's Republic of China (PRC)," she wrote, adding that "these failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI" [1] [2] . Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving them [1] . She sent the letter ahead of President Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Thursday, Nov. 19 [1] [2] . The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Monday [1] . According to The Verge, the letter says Commerce did not act on warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed's access to AI chips before reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive U.S. officials suspect of passing information to China [2] . Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 . Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last week that the Megaspeed blacklisting stalled because Commerce "has the pen" . Cantwell also criticized Commerce for letting Alibaba and ByteDance use Nvidia chips through overseas data centers and for extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain U.S. AI technology through subsidiaries, The Verge reported [2] . The New York Times reported on Nov. 15 that Lutnick pushed for narrower rules on overseas data centers serving Chinese customers . On conflicts, Cantwell said Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick led and his sons now control, held $1.2 billion of Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination [1] . She said the administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology" [1] . "America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," she wrote [1] . CNBC reported last week that Cantor held 1.81 million Nvidia shares worth $362 million at the end of June. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) has summoned Jensen Huang and Lutnick to testify in December, and Commerce spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said last week that Lutnick has agreed to appear [1] . Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have given Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller until Nov. 17 to confirm they have ordered Nvidia export records preserved [1] . Lawmakers in both parties are also moving toward tighter AI chip export rules . "The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America's most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries," Cantwell wrote in closing [2] . extraction.body: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected. "Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires. Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail. At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data… — vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026 In short, leanPCS is a proposed way for Ethereum to bundle many large, quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a single compact proof, so that the full data never has to be stored onchain. It is built on polynomial commitment schemes, or PCS, the core mathematical building block of STARK proofs. Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today. The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes. "This is unsustainable to put on chain," he wrote. Buterin's answer is EIP-8288, a draft proposal he co-authored with developer Thomas Coratger in June, which would aggregate those signatures and proofs before they ever reach a block. Under the design, users publish their signatures or proofs, and network nodes repeatedly bundle everything they have seen into a single STARK, a type of zero-knowledge proof , that attests the underlying data is valid. These aggregate proofs are themselves combined until a single "master proof" verifies everything in a block. Only short claims, rather than the full signatures or proofs, would need to be stored onchain. He laid out three ways to build it, depending on what users submit. The simplest, leanSPHINCS, would support a single type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature, costing users only a small amount of gas per signature, but it couldn't do anything else. At the other end, leanSTARK would be fully general, allowing any signature scheme, privacy protocols or hidden multisig logic. But Ethereum would first have to agree on a programming language for users' programs, which Buterin called "the first big case of 'Ethereum moving beyond the EVM,'" and which is likely to take time. Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route. It would offer the same generality as leanSTARK but "could potentially be implemented very quickly," he said, because far fewer design choices are needed, and leanSTARK could then be added later. "So there is a route to getting 'the cryptographic proof singularity' much faster than any of us expected," Buterin wrote, "and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS." Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers. The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate. Under protocol-level aggregation, a future "leanSPHINCS" verification would cost about 3,000 gas, according to the post. Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated post-quantum team in January, and Buterin has since said the network is betting its future on quantum security and privacy. Developers have also proposed overhauling the staking deposit contract to support post-quantum validator keys, and Buterin has pushed a plan to cut the cost of quantum-safe privacy. passages: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected.

"Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires.
Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.
At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data…
— vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026

In short, leanPCS is a proposed way for Ethereum to bundle many large, quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a single compact proof, so that the full data never has to be stored onchain. It is built on polynomial commitment schemes, or PCS, the core mathematical building block of STARK proofs.

Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today. The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes. "This is unsustainable to put on chain," he wrote.
Buterin's answer is EIP-8288, a draft proposal he co-authored with developer Thomas Coratger in June, which would aggregate those signatures and proofs before they ever reach a block.

Under the design, users publish their signatures or proofs, and network nodes repeatedly bundle everything they have seen into a single STARK, a type of zero-knowledge proof , that attests the underlying data is valid. These aggregate proofs are themselves combined until a single "master proof" verifies everything in a block. Only short claims, rather than the full signatures or proofs, would need to be stored onchain.

He laid out three ways to build it, depending on what users submit. The simplest, leanSPHINCS, would support a single type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature, costing users only a small amount of gas per signature, but it couldn't do anything else.

At the other end, leanSTARK would be fully general, allowing any signature scheme, privacy protocols or hidden multisig logic. But Ethereum would first have to agree on a programming language for users' programs, which Buterin called "the first big case of 'Ethereum moving beyond the EVM,'" and which is likely to take time.

Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route. It would offer the same generality as leanSTARK but "could potentially be implemented very quickly," he said, because far fewer design choices are needed, and leanSTARK could then be added later.
"So there is a route to getting 'the cryptographic proof singularity' much faster than any of us expected," Buterin wrote, "and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS."

Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers. The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate.
Under protocol-level aggregation, a future "leanSPHINCS" verification would cost about 3,000 gas, according to the post.

Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated post-quantum team in January, and Buterin has since said the network is betting its future on quantum security and privacy. Developers have also proposed overhauling the staking deposit contract to support post-quantum validator keys, and Buterin has pushed a plan to cut the cost of quantum-safe privacy.

coreStoryFacts.text: "Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires.
Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected.
Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today.

The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes.

Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers.

The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate.
Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum.
Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route.
But Ethereum would first have to agree on a programming language for users' programs, which Buterin called "the first big case of 'Ethereum moving beyond the EVM,'" and which is likely to take time.
Vitalik Buterin has reversed his view on leanPCS , backing it as a potentially faster route to a quantum-safe Ethereum upgrade.
In a November 16, 2026 post, Buterin supported a proposal that would compress bulky quantum-resistant signatures and proofs rather than store their full data onchain.
By contrast, he said leanPCS “could potentially be implemented very quickly,” with leanSTARK added later.

According to Buterin’s explainer, moving to quantum-safe cryptography would push signature sizes up from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes , while zero-knowledge proofs would expand from just a few hundred bytes to roughly 128 kilobytes .
Buterin additionally highlighted SPHINCS- , a hash-based signature family tailored for Ethereum.

Shared on the Ethereum Research forum in June with contributions from Buterin and cryptographers at the Ethereum Foundation, the work shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can be verified without any changes to the protocol.
The security problem behind the proposal extends beyond Ethereum .
Quantum computers are expected eventually to break the elliptic curve cryptography currently protecting Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts.
leanSTARK would support any signature scheme, privacy protocols, and hidden multisignature logic.
That flexibility comes with a prerequisite: Ethereum would first need to agree on a programming language for users’ programs, moving beyond the Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM.
Buterin said that process would likely take time.
Rather than storing all of the underlying data, Ethereum would keep only brief claims backed by the aggregate proof.
“Over the past few weeks I’ve gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull,” Buterin wrote.
Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has endorsed leanPCS as a key solution to enhance Ethereum's cryptographic proof scalability and security.
This initiative aligns with Ethereum's broader roadmap to improve efficiency and transition to quantum-resistant protocols.

extraction.body: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected. "Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires. Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail. At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data… — vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026 In short, leanPCS is a proposed way for Ethereum to bundle many large, quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a single compact proof, so that the full data never has to be stored onchain. It is built on polynomial commitment schemes, or PCS, the core mathematical building block of STARK proofs. Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today. The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes. "This is unsustainable to put on chain," he wrote. Buterin's answer is EIP-8288, a draft proposal he co-authored with developer Thomas Coratger in June, which would aggregate those signatures and proofs before they ever reach a block. Under the design, users publish their signatures or proofs, and network nodes repeatedly bundle everything they have seen into a single STARK, a type of zero-knowledge proof , that attests the underlying data is valid. These aggregate proofs are themselves combined until a single "master proof" verifies everything in a block. Only short claims, rather than the full signatures or proofs, would need to be stored onchain. He laid out three ways to build it, depending on what users submit. The simplest, leanSPHINCS, would support a single type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature, costing users only a small amount of gas per signature, but it couldn't do anything else. At the other end, leanSTARK would be fully general, allowing any signature scheme, privacy protocols or hidden multisig logic. But Ethereum would first have to agree on a programming language for users' programs, which Buterin called "the first big case of 'Ethereum moving beyond the EVM,'" and which is likely to take time. Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route. It would offer the same generality as leanSTARK but "could potentially be implemented very quickly," he said, because far fewer design choices are needed, and leanSTARK could then be added later. "So there is a route to getting 'the cryptographic proof singularity' much faster than any of us expected," Buterin wrote, "and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS." Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers. The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate. Under protocol-level aggregation, a future "leanSPHINCS" verification would cost about 3,000 gas, according to the post. Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated post-quantum team in January, and Buterin has since said the network is betting its future on quantum security and privacy. Developers have also proposed overhauling the staking deposit contract to support post-quantum validator keys, and Buterin has pushed a plan to cut the cost of quantum-safe privacy. passages: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected.

"Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires.
Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.
At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data…
— vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026

In short, leanPCS is a proposed way for Ethereum to bundle many large, quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a single compact proof, so that the full data never has to be stored onchain. It is built on polynomial commitment schemes, or PCS, the core mathematical building block of STARK proofs.

Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today. The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes. "This is unsustainable to put on chain," he wrote.
Buterin's answer is EIP-8288, a draft proposal he co-authored with developer Thomas Coratger in June, which would aggregate those signatures and proofs before they ever reach a block.

Under the design, users publish their signatures or proofs, and network nodes repeatedly bundle everything they have seen into a single STARK, a type of zero-knowledge proof , that attests the underlying data is valid. These aggregate proofs are themselves combined until a single "master proof" verifies everything in a block. Only short claims, rather than the full signatures or proofs, would need to be stored onchain.

He laid out three ways to build it, depending on what users submit. The simplest, leanSPHINCS, would support a single type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature, costing users only a small amount of gas per signature, but it couldn't do anything else.

At the other end, leanSTARK would be fully general, allowing any signature scheme, privacy protocols or hidden multisig logic. But Ethereum would first have to agree on a programming language for users' programs, which Buterin called "the first big case of 'Ethereum moving beyond the EVM,'" and which is likely to take time.

Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route. It would offer the same generality as leanSTARK but "could potentially be implemented very quickly," he said, because far fewer design choices are needed, and leanSTARK could then be added later.
"So there is a route to getting 'the cryptographic proof singularity' much faster than any of us expected," Buterin wrote, "and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS."

Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers. The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate.
Under protocol-level aggregation, a future "leanSPHINCS" verification would cost about 3,000 gas, according to the post.

Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated post-quantum team in January, and Buterin has since said the network is betting its future on quantum security and privacy. Developers have also proposed overhauling the staking deposit contract to support post-quantum validator keys, and Buterin has pushed a plan to cut the cost of quantum-safe privacy.

In a post on X , Buterin said he had shifted from skepticism to strong support for the approach.
Standard Ethereum signatures occupy about 65 bytes, while some quantum-resistant alternatives can require roughly 1,000 to 6,000 bytes.
The proposal aims to protect Ethereum without forcing every transaction to carry the full data cost of quantum-safe signatures.

Under the proposed design, wallets would still generate signatures proving that users authorized transactions, but network participants could combine those signatures with other cryptographic proofs before inclusion in a block.
Those batches could then be aggregated again until Ethereum stores one shared proof confirming that all underlying checks passed.
Aggregating those proofs could make advanced privacy and quantum-resistant authorization more practical without making each user pay for the full size of every proof.
It also aligns with recent calls to prioritize quantum defenses over faster block times in Ethereum’s near-term development agenda.

extraction.body: Jordanian authorities said on Monday that they will block the Telegram social media app in the kingdom over national security concerns.Jordanian Telegram users reported disruptions on Monday, according to Jordanian news outlet Roya News. Shortly after, Jordan's Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced it had blocked the messaging app nationwide.Telegram, a Dubai-based cloud messaging app for mobile and desktop, describes itself on its website as focused on security and speed. It supports end-to-end encrypted chats with self-destruct timers for sensitive messages.Jordan cites crime, extremismThe PSD said the move was meant to stop the platform from being used for cybercrime, threats, extortion, and the spread of illegal content, including extremist material, according to the Jordanian state news agency Petra.The decision comes after a rare deadly church attack last month killed nine people and prompted airstrikes on neighboring Syria that Jordan said killed 20 Islamic State terrorists. On November 5, Jordan said one security officer had been killed and another wounded in what it called a terrorist stabbing attack in Amman.Blocking Telegram is one of several measures aimed specifically at combating Islamist terrorism, Prof. Ronen Yitzhak, an expert on Jordan and head of Bar-Ilan University's Department of Multidisciplinary Studies in the Humanities, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.Jordan has intensified its war on terror, Yitzhak said, not only through counterterrorism operations, such as strikes on Islamic State strongholds in southern Syria, but also by taking the fight to social media. The move is also meant to give Jordanian citizens a renewed sense of security, he added.Barak Gonen, a cybersecurity expert and lecturer at the Jerusalem College of Technology, was more skeptical. Blocking Telegram because it was presumably used to facilitate terrorist attacks is “equivalent [to] stopping all the train transportation in the country because some terrorists are known to be on a train,” he told the Post on Monday.The move is legitimate, Gonen said, but “very extreme.”“I certainly do hope that in [Israel, the Shin Bet] has the capabilities of stopping the specific train without stopping all of the train activity in the country,” he said.Directorate encourages parents to monitor children's online activityBlocking the Telegram app aligns with Jordan's existing legislation to "protect society from the risks associated with the misuse of digital platforms," the PSD claimed, according to Petra.The directorate also urged citizens to use social media with caution, avoid interacting with suspicious accounts or unknown users, and report illegal activity. It called on parents to monitor their children's internet use, use parental controls on internet-connected devices, and “encourage safe and responsible use of technology.”Telegram did not immediately respond to The Jerusalem Post's request for comment. However, the company's automatic reply noted that “Telegram is committed to protecting user privacy and human rights such as freedom of speech and assembly.”Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, is regarded as a relatively stable state in the Middle East. Its security services have foiled plots by Islamist terrorists in the past, including suspected Islamic State supporters.Over the years, Islamic State militants have used the mobile messaging service, created by Pavel Durov, who is in exile from Russia, to issue statements.Durov faces investigations in several countries. In July, Russia said it had ​charged him with facilitating terrorist activity, alleging that his app was being used by ‌Ukrainian spies to organize attacks inside Russia.Durov denies wrongdoing and says Telegram has exceeded its obligations to moderate content and cooperate with authorities to fight crime. Iraq also moves to block TelegramLater on Monday, Iraq's Communications and Media Commission (CMC) announced that Telegram would be blocked across the country, “due to the company's failure to comply with the applicable legal and regulatory requirements.”The move is meant to push the company to review Iraqi content on the app, prevent violations, and cooperate with the commission, the CMC said, as part of wider efforts to curb the use of social media to spread extremism, incite sedition, violence, and hatred, commit cybercrime, and threaten national security.According to the CMC, Telegram did not take adequate action to combat the dissemination of content that violates Iraqi law. The commission gave Telegram a 30-day grace period to rectify the situation, although it did not specify what would happen if Telegram failed to do so.The ban comes six months after the commission lifted a week-long ban on the messaging app in May, after the company complied with the regulator's rules, according to Kurdistan Region-based news channel Rudaw Media Network. The commission had cited national security concerns then as well.The app has found a range of uses in Iraq, including by channels affiliated with pro-Iran armed groups, some of which decried Monday's decision, Rudaw reported.It also comes nearly a month after Iraq's Communications Ministry banned the navigation app Waze, citing the presence of the company's data centers in Israel, Rudaw reported.Reuters contributed to this report.

AI-generated child sexual abuse imagery has escalated by more than 8,400 per cent over a two-year timeframe, according to international research. The global investigation revealed that documented cases worldwide grew by upwards of 395,300 between 2023 and 2025. Academics also calculated that over 300 million children across the globe suffer at least one instance of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse annually. Furthermore, approximately one in four young people can expect to face some form of online abuse prior to turning 18. The statistics were compiled as part of a major international project involving Scottish experts from the Childlight Global Child Safety Institute , based at the University of Edinburgh . Childlight highlighted that referrals of AI-generated abuse material provided by technology firms to the US-based National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children surged from approximately 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The material includes “ deepfakes ”, which are created using so-called “nudify apps”, where the face of a real child can be digitally placed onto sexually explicit images in a realistic manner within seconds. Although the images may be fake, researchers said the harm to children is very real, with images sometimes used to blackmail children, demanding money or more images. Researchers said the problem affects ordinary people as well as high-profile celebrities. However, the study cautioned that changes in detection and reporting may have contributed to the dramatic increase. Professor Debi Fry, Childlight’s global director of data at Edinburgh University, said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. “These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.” She added: “While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.” Childlight’s new international study also warned that serious gaps in government data are hampering prevention efforts to protect children. Of 103 countries and areas examined across the three regions, the group said only 22 had representative survey data covering both offline and technology-facilitated abuse. According to Childlight, children with disabilities, Indigenous children, migrants, those in humanitarian settings, very young children and children abused within their families are particularly underrepresented. In response, Childlight is urging governments to treat sexual exploitation and abuse as a preventable public health issue, invest in reliable and consistent measurement, and use evidence to strengthen protection, support survivors and prevent harm before it occurs. The institute is also calling for stronger technology-sector accountability, laws that keep pace with emerging threats and prevention efforts beginning earlier in childhood. Childlight chief executive Paul Stanfield said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk. “What remains invisible risks remaining unaddressed. We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature.” Mr Stanfield, there is “nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse”. He added: “With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.” Despite the challenges, the report highlighted encouraging progress, with several countries strengthening online safety legislation, improving detection and focusing more on prevention. With better intelligence, coordinated action and sustained investment, researchers said governments have an opportunity to protect hundreds of millions of children and help create a safer future. The findings are contained in the group’s 2026 Into the Light Index, which was unveiled at a global summit involving representatives from more than 100 governments on ending violence against children on Monday.

AI-generated child sexual abuse imagery has escalated by more than 8,400 per cent over a two-year timeframe, according to international research. The global investigation revealed that documented cases worldwide grew by upwards of 395,300 between 2023 and 2025. Academics also calculated that over 300 million children across the globe suffer at least one instance of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse annually. Furthermore, approximately one in four young people can expect to face some form of online abuse prior to turning 18. The statistics were compiled as part of a major international project involving Scottish experts from the Childlight Global Child Safety Institute , based at the University of Edinburgh . Childlight highlighted that referrals of AI-generated abuse material provided by technology firms to the US-based National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children surged from approximately 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The material includes “ deepfakes ”, which are created using so-called “nudify apps”, where the face of a real child can be digitally placed onto sexually explicit images in a realistic manner within seconds. Although the images may be fake, researchers said the harm to children is very real, with images sometimes used to blackmail children, demanding money or more images. Researchers said the problem affects ordinary people as well as high-profile celebrities. However, the study cautioned that changes in detection and reporting may have contributed to the dramatic increase. Professor Debi Fry, Childlight’s global director of data at Edinburgh University, said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. “These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.” She added: “While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.” Childlight’s new international study also warned that serious gaps in government data are hampering prevention efforts to protect children. Of 103 countries and areas examined across the three regions, the group said only 22 had representative survey data covering both offline and technology-facilitated abuse. According to Childlight, children with disabilities, Indigenous children, migrants, those in humanitarian settings, very young children and children abused within their families are particularly underrepresented. In response, Childlight is urging governments to treat sexual exploitation and abuse as a preventable public health issue, invest in reliable and consistent measurement, and use evidence to strengthen protection, support survivors and prevent harm before it occurs. The institute is also calling for stronger technology-sector accountability, laws that keep pace with emerging threats and prevention efforts beginning earlier in childhood. Childlight chief executive Paul Stanfield said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk. “What remains invisible risks remaining unaddressed. We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature.” Mr Stanfield, there is “nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse”. He added: “With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.” Despite the challenges, the report highlighted encouraging progress, with several countries strengthening online safety legislation, improving detection and focusing more on prevention. With better intelligence, coordinated action and sustained investment, researchers said governments have an opportunity to protect hundreds of millions of children and help create a safer future. The findings are contained in the group’s 2026 Into the Light Index, which was unveiled at a global summit involving representatives from more than 100 governments on ending violence against children on Monday.

passages: Bitcoin's most crowded derivatives position is no longer a bet on a moonshot.
After a sharp slide, the largest single options wager on Deribit is now a put at the $60,000 strike, carrying roughly $900 million in notional open interest, according to CoinDesk.
The backdrop matters for how the positioning should be read.
Bitcoin spent much of the year climbing from roughly $64,000 to more than $85,000 during an August-September surge that concentrated open interest in upside calls.
The subsequent retreat has forced traders to reprice risk, and the options market is now split between those defending against a deeper drop and those who simply cashed out of bullish wagers.
The shift caps a turbulent stretch for the largest cryptocurrency.
Bitcoin fell as far as the low $60,000s before recovering to trade around $64,000, a bounce that suggests buyers are stepping in at lower levels but has yet to produce a convincing breakout.
For investors, the practical signal is less about a forecast of $60,000 than about where protection is concentrated.
A large put strike can act as a magnet for hedging flows and amplify moves as expiry approaches, but it does not by itself dictate spot prices.
The contract pays off if bitcoin trades below $60,000, making it a form of insurance against further losses.
Nicolas Quatravaux, head of EMEA at Paradigm, a crypto derivatives liquidity network, cautioned that the headline number says more about the past than the present.
"OI is a stock, not a flow; it shows what's been built up over months, not what people are doing today," he said.

The size is tracking spot and sitting just above $60,000 rather than on it, Quatravaux said, with two-way trading and put spreads such as 60/64 changing hands in smaller clips around that level.
Other flows point to more nuanced positioning.

That trade profits from a sharp decline but not from a decline alone, with maximum loss at expiry near $68,000 and break-even prices around $62,380 and $70,650.
Put diagonal spreads, designed to profit from a controlled or gradual decline into mid-to-late November, also drew interest.

The contract pays off if bitcoin trades below $60,000, making it a form of insurance against further losses. It displaced the $100,000 call, which had held the top spot through the late-summer rally and now sits second with about $867 million in open interest. The shift caps a turbulent stretch for the largest cryptocurrency. Bitcoin fell as far as the low $60,000s before recovering to trade around $64,000, a bounce that suggests buyers are stepping in at lower levels but has yet to produce a convincing breakout. The $64,000 zone is now the first technical hurdle on the upside; a failure there would put the $62,000 support back in play, with a break below opening the door to $60,000. Note: One Deribit contract represents one bitcoin. Nicolas Quatravaux, head of EMEA at Paradigm, a crypto derivatives liquidity network, cautioned that the headline number says more about the past than the present. The $60,000 put has been the go-to protection strike all year, he told CoinDesk, with heavy buying on Paradigm whenever the market wobbled in February, March and again in June. "OI is a stock, not a flow; it shows what's been built up over months, not what people are doing today," he said. The call's demotion, meanwhile, reflects position unwinding rather than a rush into bearish bets. Traders bought more than 12,000 BTC of $100,000 calls on Paradigm in September during the squeeze and sold back roughly 6,700 BTC of them in October, according to Quatravaux. "So the 100k call didn't lose the top spot because everyone rushed into puts; it's more that the upside bets got taken off," he said. Recent put activity has been dominated by a single large player rolling a sizable position to progressively lower strikes as spot price declined, from $74,000 in late October through $72,000, $68,000, $65,000 and $63,000 by the end of November, amounting to more than $1 billion of put blocks on Paradigm in two days. The size is tracking spot and sitting just above $60,000 rather than on it, Quatravaux said, with two-way trading and put spreads such as 60/64 changing hands in smaller clips around that level. Other flows point to more nuanced positioning. Volmex's bitcoin 30-day implied volatility index, BVIV, jumped to 57.13 points on Sunday, its highest since June, before retreating to 44 as the initial panic faded. A large put strike can act as a magnet for hedging flows and amplify moves as expiry approaches, but it does not by itself dictate spot prices. What matters over the coming sessions is whether bitcoin can hold above $64,000 and keep the $62,000 support intact; a decisive break lower would test the conviction of the traders who have spent months building positions around the $60,000 level. Puts, which give holders the right to sell at a predetermined price, are often used as protection when further drops are expected. The positioning follows an especially sharp drop in Bitcoin last week, which saw the largest digital asset fall by 12%. It hit a four-month low of nearly $62,000 over the weekend before clawing back some of those losses. In the options market, traders remain wary. "Market participants were looking to hedge short-term downside risk via options in very thin liquidity," said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. During the selloff, a gauge comparing the pricing of puts and calls expiring Friday reached 25 points in favor of puts, according to Mauron. That showed strong demand for protection against a further drop. "The $60,000 level has been established as a strong support, holding up twice this year as well as throughout 2024," Mauron said. A decisive break below that level could inflict serious pain on the market, she added, with no obvious support before $40,000. Bitcoin briefly fell through $60,000 on July 1, hitting a low of $57,742 for the year, but it has traded above that level since July 2. The token's latest swoon has come as several of the forces that once helped push it higher have reversed. Investors have pulled almost $3 billion from US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds since the $6 billion Binance hack on Oct. 29, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The outflows have removed a source of demand that had helped underpin the cryptocurrency. At the same time, the outlook for US interest rates has turned more negative. Traders have added to bets on further Federal Reserve rate increases in 2027 and have begun assigning a small probability to a half-percentage-point increase in December after inflation again topped forecasts. Crypto has also been swept up in a broader retreat from risk assets, fueled by turmoil around the artificial-intelligence trade. "The problem is that Bitcoin is competing for attention in a crowded macro environment," said Robin Singh, chief executive officer of Koinly. "Between the Nvidia controversy, growing economic uncertainty and geopolitical tensions, investors have plenty of other things to worry about." That leaves Bitcoin short of an obvious catalyst to draw buyers back in, according to Singh, who said the cryptocurrency could struggle to rebuild momentum. To be sure, Jeff Ko, chief analyst at ViaBTC, said Bitcoin may be nearing a turning point. "Much of the recent decline presumably reflects capital rotating into Anthropic's IPO, as investors sold liquid assets to fund their allocations," he said, adding the token saw a similar selloff ahead of the SpaceX IPO and then rebounded quickly. "The drop to $62,000 over the weekend also flushed out a large share of leveraged speculative positions," Ko said. "I think that gives a healthier base for a recovery." For now, technical indicators offer little comfort. The latest decline brought Bitcoin back below its 200-day and 200-week moving averages — levels seen as key long-term indicators. That "paints a bearish picture in the short term," according to Pratik Kala, a portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto. This leaves options traders focused on a support level that has already shown resilience twice this year, with hopes that it may pull off a third rebound.

The positioning matters because hedges can shape how the price moves as it nears key levels. Bitcoin has struggled to hold any bounce this month. Traders now want to know whether buyers can defend the first floor or whether put holders will collect. Demand has grown for contracts that pay out if the price falls toward $60,000. No single fund or trader stands behind the move. The flow looks like broad hedging across the market. The week explains the caution. Bitcoin lost about 14% over seven days, and each bounce faded quickly. Buyers who stepped in early were left holding losses. Many holders now prefer insurance over fresh bets on a rebound. That shift matters for how the market trades. Downside protection has become the crowded position, and crowded positions shape behavior. Traders who sold or bought those puts will adjust their hedges as the price nears the strike. The round number now works as a target for bears and a test of nerve for everyone else. Bitcoin traded near $64,000 at last check, and the broader chart looks heavy. The price sits under both of the moving averages that traders use to judge the long trend. A moving average smooths out daily swings to show the typical price over a set period. The 50-day average stands near $77,000. The 200-day average sits just below it. Both lines hover well above the current price. They now act as ceilings, levels where past buyers may sell to break even. The shorter average has slipped toward the longer one, which shows that recent weeks were weaker than the past several months. Sellers have controlled the trend for a while, and each rally has stalled long before reaching those lines. The monthly picture adds to the strain. Bitcoin fell about 21% over the past 30 days. That decline leaves the price pinned near the bottom of its range for the month, with little cushion from recent lows. A recovery would be hard. Bitcoin would need to climb roughly $12,000 just to touch the 200-day line. A move that size would take sustained buying, and buyers have shown little of it so far. RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, reads about 22 on the daily chart. Anything below 30 counts as oversold. That means the selling has run far and fast, and readings this low often come before a relief bounce. An oversold reading alone is a weak reason to buy. In strong downtrends, RSI can stay pinned near the floor for days while the price keeps sliding. Traders usually wait for the gauge to turn higher before trusting a rebound. Other signals still favor the bears. The MACD, a tool that tracks shifts in momentum, remains below its signal line, so momentum is still pointing down. Trend strength readings confirm a real trend, and sellers are leading it. Recent trading offered a small hint of relief. Bitcoin slipped only about 1% over the past day, a far gentler pace than earlier in the week. That suggests the pressure may be easing. It does not yet show buyers taking control. The first floor sits near $62,000, just below the current price. Buyers defended this area recently, so it is the first real test for the bears. A daily close beneath it would show that demand has thinned out. If that floor gives way, the next support waits near $59,000. That level sits just under the options target. A slide there would hand the put buyers their payout and could trigger more hedging as dealers adjust. Overhead, the first resistance stands near $75,000, close to both long averages. Bitcoin would need to reclaim that zone to break the bearish case. A move back above it would leave the downside contracts looking like expensive insurance. The second ceiling sits near $80,000. A climb through that level would confirm a full trend reversal. Sellers would lose control, and the options crowd would need a new plan. The next three days should show whether the selloff runs its course or reaches the bears' target. The bias stays bearish until Bitcoin climbs back above its long averages. Sellers still drive the trend, and the put buyers' target sits only a short drop away. Late bears face a real risk, though. Deeply oversold markets can snap higher without warning. A sharp short squeeze would punish traders who piled into downside bets near the lows. Disclaimer: This article is provided for informational purposes only. Bitcoin plunged to a four-month low near $62,000 on Sunday, Nov. 15 as heavy selling in dollar-denominated markets intensified a broader cryptocurrency downturn. Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 on Nov. 15, its weakest level since July, before rebounding. Binance Research said the decline extended BTC's losses to 15.6% over 11 days, which is its sharpest comparable selloff since June. The selling pressure has pushed Bitcoin into a price region that on-chain analytics firm Glassnode had identified as particularly vulnerable. Glassnode reported that Bitcoin had entered the upper boundary of its largest concentration of potential liquidations between $60,000 and $63,000, a zone it had warned about for weeks. During the weekend selloff, CoinGlass recorded nearly $2 billion in liquidations across the crypto market over 24 hours. Bitcoin's latest downturn has exposed a striking disparity in selling pressure between dollar-denominated trading venues and Binance , suggesting risk aversion is particularly pronounced in USD markets. Between Nov. 11 and Nov. 14, aggressive selling exceeded buying by 7,438 BTC on a major dollar-based spot exchange, compared with 2,707 BTC on Binance, according to Binance Research . The reported selling imbalance on the unnamed USD venue was about 2.75 times Binance’s. The pressure has also coincided with substantial withdrawals from US-listed investment products. US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded nearly $2 billion in net outflows across seven consecutive sessions from Nov. 5 through Nov. 13, according to Farside Investors . Binance Research linked the simultaneous pressures to mounting uncertainty over interest rates, dollar liquidity and the sustainability of the artificial intelligence investment boom. The concerns have coincided with upheaval at Nvidia, where Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as chief executive on Nov. 12, leaving longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO as investors scrutinize the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending ahead of Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. However, Strive CEO Matt Cole believes Bitcoin's current weakness resembles the conditions surrounding SpaceX's record-breaking public offering earlier this year. Cole observed that Bitcoin declined 19% over the 50 days before SpaceX's June 12 listing , closely resembling the 18% decline ahead of Anthropic's planned IPO when he made the comparison on Nov. 13. Anthropic’s proposed offering could total about $64 billion at the top of its indicated price range, including shares sold by existing holders. Cole noted that Bitcoin continued declining after SpaceX's listing, reaching its lowest point 18 days later before staging a sharp recovery. By the 100th day after the offering, the cryptocurrency had gained 28% from its IPO-day closing price and 39% from its subsequent low. His chart sketches Bitcoin near $90,000 by late February 2027 if the post-SpaceX price pattern repeats after Anthropic’s listing. The comparison offers a competing interpretation of the current downturn, although the similarities do not establish that either public offering caused Bitcoin's decline. The earlier episode also suggests that additional losses could precede any sustained recovery. The next test comes on Nov. 16 when US spot Bitcoin ETFs reopen after seven consecutive sessions of withdrawals, followed by Nvidia's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17. Bitcoin plunged to a four-month low near $62,000 on Sunday, Nov. 15 as heavy selling in dollar-denominated markets intensified a broader cryptocurrency downturn.

Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 on Nov. 15, its weakest level since July, before rebounding. Binance Research said the decline extended BTC's losses to 15.6% over 11 days, which is its sharpest comparable selloff since June.
The selling pressure has pushed Bitcoin into a price region that on-chain analytics firm Glassnode had identified as particularly vulnerable.
Glassnode reported that Bitcoin had entered the upper boundary of its largest concentration of potential liquidations between $60,000 and $63,000, a zone it had warned about for weeks.
During the weekend selloff, CoinGlass recorded nearly $2 billion in liquidations across the crypto market over 24 hours.

Bitcoin's latest downturn has exposed a striking disparity in selling pressure between dollar-denominated trading venues and Binance , suggesting risk aversion is particularly pronounced in USD markets.
Between Nov. 11 and Nov. 14, aggressive selling exceeded buying by 7,438 BTC on a major dollar-based spot exchange, compared with 2,707 BTC on Binance, according to Binance Research .
The reported selling imbalance on the unnamed USD venue was about 2.75 times Binance’s.

The pressure has also coincided with substantial withdrawals from US-listed investment products. US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded nearly $2 billion in net outflows across seven consecutive sessions from Nov. 5 through Nov. 13, according to Farside Investors .
Binance Research linked the simultaneous pressures to mounting uncertainty over interest rates, dollar liquidity and the sustainability of the artificial intelligence investment boom.

The concerns have coincided with upheaval at Nvidia, where Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as chief executive on Nov. 12, leaving longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO as investors scrutinize the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending ahead of Anthropic's blockbuster IPO.
However, Strive CEO Matt Cole believes Bitcoin's current weakness resembles the conditions surrounding SpaceX's record-breaking public offering earlier this year.
Cole observed that Bitcoin declined 19% over the 50 days before SpaceX's June 12 listing , closely resembling the 18% decline ahead of Anthropic's planned IPO when he made the comparison on Nov. 13.
Anthropic’s proposed offering could total about $64 billion at the top of its indicated price range, including shares sold by existing holders.

Cole noted that Bitcoin continued declining after SpaceX's listing, reaching its lowest point 18 days later before staging a sharp recovery. By the 100th day after the offering, the cryptocurrency had gained 28% from its IPO-day closing price and 39% from its subsequent low.
His chart sketches Bitcoin near $90,000 by late February 2027 if the post-SpaceX price pattern repeats after Anthropic’s listing.

The comparison offers a competing interpretation of the current downturn, although the similarities do not establish that either public offering caused Bitcoin's decline. The earlier episode also suggests that additional losses could precede any sustained recovery.
The next test comes on Nov. 16 when US spot Bitcoin ETFs reopen after seven consecutive sessions of withdrawals, followed by Nvidia's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.

The move capped a sharp reversal from the $58,293 low Bitcoin touched on July 1. A softer-than-expected jobs report reshaped rate-hike expectations heading into the new week, helping Bitcoin’s price claw back. The rally traces back to Thursday’s US Nonfarm Payrolls report . The report showed the economy added just 57,000 jobs in June, far below forecasts. The miss lowered the odds of a near-term Federal Reserve rate hike, and Bitcoin had already gained ground on Warsh’s inflation risk comments earlier in the week. Lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar reduced the opportunity cost of holding Bitcoin, helping the asset recover from a bearish June. Spot Bitcoin ETFs added to the momentum. An ETF inflow reversal snapped a 10-day run of redemptions, though the funds are still working through June’s record outflows of $4.5 billion. A weekend of rising price action was capped by a spike towards $64,000. Image Source: BeInCrypto Traders lost over $450 million in short positions across the derivatives market as Bitcoin broke through $62,000. Bitcoin’s price reflected the broader squeeze dynamic, in which forced buybacks push the price into the next tranche of shorts. Ether rose roughly 4% on the day and about 10% over the week, while Solana added nearly 19%, the strongest gain among major tokens. Institutional flows have not fully confirmed the move, with ETFs still recovering from their worst month on record. Whether the squeeze becomes a durable trend remains an open question. Forced short-covering tends to produce fast price moves rather than sustained demand. The market now enters the third quarter with thinner liquidity, a dynamic that could cut in either direction. The world’s largest cryptocurrency is trying to hold its ground after a weekend plunge to $62,000, as tech stocks slid ahead of Nvidia’s earnings and traders braced for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month.
The selling that broke Friday’s low on Saturday morning did not stop there.
Bitcoin slipped under $64,000 Saturday afternoon and dropped below $62,000 in the 8 p.m.
ET hour on some exchanges, its lowest level since July 14.
It bounced back above $64,800 within the hour and reached about $66,100 early Sunday before sellers returned.

The slide has been punishing for leveraged traders. About $2 billion of crypto positions were liquidated over a 24-hour period during the weekend, the vast majority of them long bets. Bitcoin is now down 17% in November and has posted six straight weekly losses. Stock futures offered little help on Monday. Contracts on the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.5% and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.7%, while Nvidia fell 3% in premarket trading. Investors weighed a Financial Times report that former CEO Jensen Huang and his allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him, a week after his resignation sent bitcoin below $72,000 . Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, and options markets imply an earnings-day move of about 7% in either direction, Pepperstone’s Chris Weston told Reuters. Bitcoin has traded in step with chip stocks for much of the past week, so a weak report could add to the pressure. Rates remain the other weight on the bitcoin price. Traders fully price a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December meeting, with odds of a half-point move near 8%, CME FedWatch data show. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.12% on Monday after jumping 29 basis points last week, and higher yields have lifted the dollar to its strongest level since April 2025. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks in San Francisco later Monday, and minutes from the last Fed meeting are due Wednesday. Bitcoin-linked stocks fell with the coin. Strategy (MSTR) was down 8% in premarket trading and Strive (ASST) fell 9%. Strategy is also facing index-fund selling after MSCI removed it from its USA index , forcing index funds to sell by Nov. 30. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed another $185 million on Friday, their seventh straight day of outflows, bringing losses since Nov. 5 to about $1.91 billion. That run follows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bleeding $2 billion over nine straight sessions. Analysts are now focused on the $60,000 level, which marked the lows of February and June. John Roque, technical strategist at 22V Research, said bitcoin is close to completing a head-and-shoulders top. “Bitcoin has not broken below its neckline at 60,000,” he wrote in a note Saturday, adding that such a breach “would then imply risk to $38,000.” Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co., wrote that bitcoin “NEEDS to hold the $60k level,” warning that “any material break below that level would be quite bearish.” A gauge of bitcoin’s 30-day implied volatility climbed to 49.75 over the weekend, its highest since June. With Nvidia’s report, Fed speakers and the Fed minutes all due in the next three days, the bitcoin price faces a busy week. A move back above $66,000 would recover Sunday’s bounce high, while a break below the weekend low near $62,000 would put the $60,000 floor in play. The world’s largest cryptocurrency is trying to hold its ground after a weekend plunge to $62,000, as tech stocks slid ahead of Nvidia’s earnings and traders braced for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month.

ET hour on some exchanges, its lowest level since July 14.
It bounced back above $64,800 within the hour and reached about $66,100 early Sunday before sellers returned.

extraction.body: Bitcoin price traded near $64,000 on Monday morning, down about 2% from Sunday, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The world’s largest cryptocurrency is trying to hold its ground after a weekend plunge to $62,000, as tech stocks slid ahead of Nvidia’s earnings and traders braced for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month. The selling that broke Friday’s low on Saturday morning did not stop there. Bitcoin slipped under $64,000 Saturday afternoon and dropped below $62,000 in the 8 p.m. ET hour on some exchanges, its lowest level since July 14. It bounced back above $64,800 within the hour and reached about $66,100 early Sunday before sellers returned. The bitcoin price has spent most of the past day between $64,000 and $65,000. The slide has been punishing for leveraged traders. About $2 billion of crypto positions were liquidated over a 24-hour period during the weekend, the vast majority of them long bets. Bitcoin is now down 17% in November and has posted six straight weekly losses. Stock futures offered little help on Monday. Contracts on the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.5% and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.7%, while Nvidia fell 3% in premarket trading. Investors weighed a Financial Times report that former CEO Jensen Huang and his allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him, a week after his resignation sent bitcoin below $72,000 . Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, and options markets imply an earnings-day move of about 7% in either direction, Pepperstone’s Chris Weston told Reuters. Bitcoin has traded in step with chip stocks for much of the past week, so a weak report could add to the pressure. Rates remain the other weight on the bitcoin price. Traders fully price a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December meeting, with odds of a half-point move near 8%, CME FedWatch data show. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.12% on Monday after jumping 29 basis points last week, and higher yields have lifted the dollar to its strongest level since April 2025. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks in San Francisco later Monday, and minutes from the last Fed meeting are due Wednesday. Bitcoin-linked stocks fell with the coin. Strategy (MSTR) was down 8% in premarket trading and Strive (ASST) fell 9%. Strategy is also facing index-fund selling after MSCI removed it from its USA index , forcing index funds to sell by Nov. 30. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed another $185 million on Friday, their seventh straight day of outflows, bringing losses since Nov. 5 to about $1.91 billion. That run follows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bleeding $2 billion over nine straight sessions. Analysts are now focused on the $60,000 level, which marked the lows of February and June. John Roque, technical strategist at 22V Research, said bitcoin is close to completing a head-and-shoulders top. “Bitcoin has not broken below its neckline at 60,000,” he wrote in a note Saturday, adding that such a breach “would then imply risk to $38,000.” Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co., wrote that bitcoin “NEEDS to hold the $60k level,” warning that “any material break below that level would be quite bearish.” A gauge of bitcoin’s 30-day implied volatility climbed to 49.75 over the weekend, its highest since June. With Nvidia’s report, Fed speakers and the Fed minutes all due in the next three days, the bitcoin price faces a busy week. A move back above $66,000 would recover Sunday’s bounce high, while a break below the weekend low near $62,000 would put the $60,000 floor in play. At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $64,100. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. 16, citing the platform's use to facilitate cybercrime, extremism and activities that threaten national security [1] .

Telegram users in Jordan reported widespread disruptions before the announcement, Roya News reported [1] .

Telegram, founded by Pavel Durov and based in Dubai, did not respond to The Jerusalem Post's request for comment; an automatic reply said the company "is committed to protecting user privacy and human rights such as freedom of speech and assembly" [2] .
Islamic State militants have used the app to issue statements over the years, and Russia said in July that it had charged Durov with facilitating terrorist activity, which he denies [2] .
Vietnam ordered telecom providers to block Telegram in May 2025, saying the company had not cooperated with criminal investigations; Telegram said it was surprised by the move [4] .
The statement did not name specific incidents.
5, Jordan said one security officer was killed and another wounded in what it called a terrorist stabbing attack in Amman [3] .

extraction.body: LeoLabs has acquired FishEye Software as a wholly owned subsidiary, the company announced in a release dated November 16, 2026, to accelerate delivery of next-generation radars for missile warning and tracking. Financial terms were not disclosed. LeoLabs funded the transaction with proceeds from a loan provided by Hercules Capital ( HTGC ) . FishEye is an engineering-services company specializing in mission-critical U.S. government defense systems. It brings nearly 30 years of experience in systems engineering, software development and field testing for government-owned-and-operated radars supporting space domain awareness and missile defense. The acquisition adds dozens of U.S. security-cleared systems engineers, software developers and radar experts , according to LeoLabs’ announcement summary. Chief Executive Tony Frazier made the software-integration rationale explicit: “FishEye brings decades of experience developing and integrating software for U.S. missile defense systems. That expertise will help us continue to adapt our proven radar technology for missile warning and tracking, and move those capabilities into operational use quickly.” The acquisition follows LeoLabs’ October 29, 2026 announcement of more than $100 million in 2026 bookings across U.S. and Allied customers. The company attributed the growth to accelerating demand for its next-generation radars supporting space superiority and missile defense. It is expanding capacity to build and field multiple radars concurrently. LeoLabs Seeker and Scout systems were already moving through its U.S. manufacturing line for delivery in 2027. The production ramp uses an established U.S. supply chain of contract manufacturers and component suppliers to increase output while maintaining delivery timelines. The additional capacity is intended to support both LeoLabs’ company-owned-and-operated radar network and sovereign systems delivered to government customers. Hiring is another part of that expansion. The October announcement described accelerated recruitment across radar and software engineering, manufacturing, systems integration and operations, with plans to nearly double the employee base by the end of 2026. FishEye adds an established engineering team to that broader build-out. The Hercules acquisition loan is separate from the up to $150 million conditional loan commitment LeoLabs announced on November 5, 2026, from the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital. That commitment is intended to expand U.S. radar manufacturing, strengthen the domestic supply chain and accelerate deployment of sensing infrastructure for national-security missions. The manufacturing expansion supported by the commitment includes completing two large-scale facilities by 2028 and adding dozens of radar systems to LeoLabs’ global network by 2030. It is also intended to expand deliveries of sovereign radars to U.S. and Allied government customers. The Office of Strategic Capital announcement identifies the transportable Scout-X as optimized for missile warning and tracking, the mission at the center of the FishEye acquisition. The deal therefore adds software, integration and field-test expertise to a wider production and financing effort. For LeoLabs, the central execution task is to combine FishEye’s engineering resources with its manufacturing build-out and convert booked demand into operational radars on the timelines it has set. Financial terms were not disclosed. LeoLabs funded the transaction with proceeds from a loan provided by Hercules Capital ( HTGC ) . FishEye is an engineering-services company specializing in mission-critical U.S. government defense systems. It brings nearly 30 years of experience in systems engineering, software development and field testing for government-owned-and-operated radars supporting space domain awareness and missile defense. The acquisition adds dozens of U.S. security-cleared systems engineers, software developers and radar experts , according to LeoLabs’ announcement summary. Chief Executive Tony Frazier made the software-integration rationale explicit: “FishEye brings decades of experience developing and integrating software for U.S. missile defense systems.
