It is expanding capacity to build and field multiple radars concurrently. LeoLabs Seeker and Scout systems were already moving through its U.S. manufacturing line for delivery in 2027. The production ramp uses an established U.S. supply chain of contract manufacturers and component suppliers to increase output while maintaining delivery timelines. The additional capacity is intended to support both LeoLabs’ company-owned-and-operated radar network and sovereign systems delivered to government customers. Hiring is another part of that expansion. The October announcement described accelerated recruitment across radar and software engineering, manufacturing, systems integration and operations, with plans to nearly double the employee base by the end of 2026. FishEye adds an established engineering team to that broader build-out. The Hercules acquisition loan is separate from the up to $150 million conditional loan commitment LeoLabs announced on November 5, 2026, from the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital. That commitment is intended to expand U.S. radar manufacturing, strengthen the domestic supply chain and accelerate deployment of sensing infrastructure for national-security missions. The manufacturing expansion supported by the commitment includes completing two large-scale facilities by 2028 and adding dozens of radar systems to LeoLabs’ global network by 2030. It is also intended to expand deliveries of sovereign radars to U.S. and Allied government customers. The Office of Strategic Capital announcement identifies the transportable Scout-X as optimized for missile warning and tracking, the mission at the center of the FishEye acquisition. The deal therefore adds software, integration and field-test expertise to a wider production and financing effort. For LeoLabs, the central execution task is to combine FishEye’s engineering resources with its manufacturing build-out and convert booked demand into operational radars on the timelines it has set. sources.title: Apple Reboots Its Smart-Home Strategy With New Hardware and a ‘Home Collection’
passages: But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.” This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40).

But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.
That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.
The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support.
The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.
It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store.
You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad.
It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black.
The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks.

extraction.body: But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned. That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras. The Apple HomeView The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple. It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.) Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad. We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. The Apple Home Collection One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.” This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40). These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off. The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada. The HomePod Mini 2 Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis. Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black. One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing. It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface. You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer. Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10. The Apple TV 4K Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor. But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299. Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version. Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone. The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content. The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.

passages: To say this is an important development would be a colossal understatement.
The execution of this feature is the core of Apple’s game plan for the next few years, when it intends to release numerous products that leverage its iPhone app ecosystem to power Siri AI.
Apple needs software makers to begin preparing for what it hopes will be its flagship new product of 2027: smart glasses built around Siri AI, code-named N50.
These devices don’t make a lot of sense unless there’s a useful AI assistant behind them.
Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses, I’m told.
The idea is to make those apps available through Siri, allowing users to get things done without grabbing their phones.

Apple believes its large developer ecosystem could give it an advantage over Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, potentially providing countless third-party integrations when the glasses go on sale.

extraction.body: But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned. That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras. The Apple HomeView The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple. It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.) Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad. We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. The Apple Home Collection One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.” This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40). These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off. The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada. The HomePod Mini 2 Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis. Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black. One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing. It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface. You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer. Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10. The Apple TV 4K Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor. But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299. Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version. Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone. The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content. The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.

The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks.

With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off.
The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada.
The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada.

The HomePod Mini 2 Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales.
The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30.
That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis.

Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2).
It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black.
One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing.
It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface.
You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer.
Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10.
The Apple TV 4K Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor.
But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299.

Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version.

Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone.
The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content.
The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.
extraction.headline: Apple Reboots Its Smart-Home Strategy With New Hardware and a ‘Home Collection’
extraction.description: I got an early glimpse of Apple’s biggest push into the smart home in years.

relevantPassages.text: But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.” This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40).

But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.
That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.
The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support.
The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.
It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store.
You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad.

sources.title: Siri AI and iPhone apps are the cornerstones of Apple’s hardware strategy - Six Colors
passages: To say this is an important development would be a colossal understatement.
The execution of this feature is the core of Apple’s game plan for the next few years, when it intends to release numerous products that leverage its iPhone app ecosystem to power Siri AI.
Apple needs software makers to begin preparing for what it hopes will be its flagship new product of 2027: smart glasses built around Siri AI, code-named N50.
These devices don’t make a lot of sense unless there’s a useful AI assistant behind them.
Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses, I’m told.
The idea is to make those apps available through Siri, allowing users to get things done without grabbing their phones.

Apple believes its large developer ecosystem could give it an advantage over Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, potentially providing countless third-party integrations when the glasses go on sale.

extraction.body: Earlier this month, Apple rolled out its Siri AI Developer Preview , which lays the groundwork for developers to allow their apps to be controlled in a fairly sophisticated fashion by Apple’s AI assistant. To say this is an important development would be a colossal understatement. The execution of this feature is the core of Apple’s game plan for the next few years, when it intends to release numerous products that leverage its iPhone app ecosystem to power Siri AI. Apple’s latest new product, the HomeView , is built around Siri AI. (It’s a light dash of Siri AI right now, but its links with content on individual iPhones show what the company is envisioning there.) The new Apple TV 4K has added microphones to make it an additional home access point for Siri AI. And there’s much more to come, as reported by Mark Gurman at Bloomberg : Apple needs software makers to begin preparing for what it hopes will be its flagship new product of 2027: smart glasses built around Siri AI, code-named N50. Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses, I’m told. The idea is to make those apps available through Siri, allowing users to get things done without grabbing their phones. Apple believes its large developer ecosystem could give it an advantage over Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, potentially providing countless third-party integrations when the glasses go on sale. Gurman expects the Siri-powered glasses (which are basically AirPods you wear on your face) to be released at WWDC , with a similar set of AirPods armed with AI-powered cameras set to debut later in the year. ( We’ll see .) These devices don’t make a lot of sense unless there’s a useful AI assistant behind them. Siri AI is not quite that yet—it’s more reliable and more useful than the old Siri was, but it’s not as good as it should be, and it’s sometimes very slow—but at least it’s promising. Still, just as the iPhone would be a lot less appealing if it only ran Apple-built apps, Siri AI is less appealing if it doesn’t have access to the functionality of the app ecosystem. Currently, Siri AI can use Spotlight to search content offered by third-party apps, but what it can’t do is learn about functionality offered by individual apps and command those apps to perform those functions in service of a larger request. That’s the goal of the Siri AI Developer Preview—and that sort of stuff is what’s going to make the HomeView (let alone glasses or AirPods paired with an iPhone) a more appealing product. If Apple can’t pull this off, well, it calls into question the trajectory of Apple’s entire future product strategy. There’s no point in making amazing hardware if there’s nothing running on it that appeals. If you appreciate articles like this one, support us by becoming a Six Colors subscriber . extraction.body: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition. Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else. These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy. The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem. Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve. I spoke to Leo Wang , the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai , this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China. Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said. Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap. “If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.” When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing. “If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.” May Mobility plans to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company said it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.) Newmo , a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI. ParkBee , a Dutch parking technology company, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations. Port , an urban logistics company, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord. Lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency said that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District. The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end , according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck. Tesla is expanding its robotaxi service to San Antonio, Texas, as it seeks to compete with Waymo and position itself as more than just an automaker. Uber is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero. Meanwhile, the company is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. United Airlines will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf. extraction.body: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition. Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else. These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy. The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem. Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve. I spoke to Leo Wang , the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai , this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China. Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said. Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap. “If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.” When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing. “If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.” May Mobility plans to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company said it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.) Newmo , a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI. ParkBee , a Dutch parking technology company, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations. Port , an urban logistics company, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord. Lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency said that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District. The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end , according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck. Tesla is expanding its robotaxi service to San Antonio, Texas, as it seeks to compete with Waymo and position itself as more than just an automaker. Uber is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero. Meanwhile, the company is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. United Airlines will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf. This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology. How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , our series “ Are we there yet? ” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises. We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten. Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise. Nuclear-powered spaceships Exercise in a pill Interspecies communication Solid-state batteries Cleaning up PFAS Eliminating traffic deaths Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality. Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion tomorrow. extraction.body: Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country. Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy , says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs. That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023. Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid. “We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.” Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,0000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments. Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models. The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said. To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added. Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said. The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital. Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth.

Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.
Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells.
To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions.
Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface.

sources.title: Apple's New Research App Is Designed To Make AI Health Tools More User-Friendly - Engadget
passages: Apple has unveiled a new research study with the aim of learning how people use AI health tools in order to make them more effective and user-friendly.

The company is launching the Health AI Usage Study in conjunction with OpenEvidence , a clinical AI platform used by health professionals that draws medical data from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine .
Participants will use the app to ask medical questions via text-based prompts like "how can I improve my heart health," according to the app's screen shots.
They'll then receive non-jargony responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources.
A key part of the research is a new app now available for download , with Apple aiming to have up to 200,000 participants.
Users must live in the US and be 21 or older, and have an iPhone 15 Pro or later model running iOS 26 and up.
They can choose to share (or not) Apple HealthKit data, including activity levels, sleep quality and lab results, for extra context around their health.
Apple notes that the app is not integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence, and said that participant data will remain confidential and won't be used to train AI models.
"[We] believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding," said Apple VP of Health and fitness Sumbul Desai, MD, in a statement.

"Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey."

Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life.

Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. passages: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.

The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.

The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.

Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.

Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”

The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week .

sources.title: Amazon's Zoox partners with Uber to reach more robotaxi riders — first in Las Vegas, then LA - CNBC
passages: Amazon 's Zoox is making its toaster-shaped self-driving vehicles available through the Uber app in Las Vegas starting this summer, the latest sign of momentum in the nascent but fast-growing robotaxi market.
"This partnership is an opportunity to continue advancing the use of autonomous mobility in daily life," Zoox CEO Aicha Evans said in a statement.
"Through our collaboration, Zoox will provide a differentiated rider experience to those who already know and love the convenience of riding with Uber."
Amazon, which acquired Zoox in 2020, is way behind Alphabet's Waymo, the U.S. robotaxi leader.
Waymo said in February that it had surpassed 400,000 weekly rides across six U.S. metro areas.
It's now operating its service commercially in 10 U.S. cities, and aiming for expansion to London and Tokyo in 2026.
Zoox began offering free driverless rides last year around the Las Vegas Strip and certain San Francisco neighborhoods.
While it's served more than 300,000 riders, the company said in early March it's not yet offering paid rides.
Earlier this week, Zoox announced an expansion of its testing efforts across some cities in the South.

During Uber's fourth-quarter earnings call in February, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told analysts that AVs available via his company's app attain "significantly higher utilization" than robotaxis hailed on "stand-alone platforms," basing those estimates on unspecified publicly available data.
Trips per AV, per day are 30% higher on Uber, Khosrowshahi said.
As first-party robotaxi brand services and apps become more familiar to travelers and commuters, they could take market share away from Uber and rivals like Lyft or DiDi in China.
Zoox is seeking an exemption from U.S. regulators to commercially deploy its robotaxis.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Tuesday opened up public comments on Zoox's petition, which seeks permission to operate up to 2,500 vehicles on U.S. roads.
As part of a multiyear partnership announced Wednesday, the companies said they plan to make Zoox rides available in Los Angeles next year.
In both cities, Zoox will continue to offer rides on its own app as well.
The Zoox robotaxis have been nicknamed "toasters" due to their shape, with a low step, doors that automatically open and close, and seats that face each other.
Regulators previously gave approval for Zoox to deploy its custom-built vehicles for research and demonstration purposes only.
For Uber, the alliance comes as executives pitch the company's platform as the best way for autonomous vehicle makers to tap rider demand.

sources.title: Amazon’s Zoox robotaxis are now available via Uber
passages: Zoox plans to launch initial standalone operations in LA through its own app before the end of 2026, followed by a full Uber integration sometime in 2027.
Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a new robotaxi BFF: Amazon.
Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis.

It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app.
Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge.

MGM, Uber, and Zoox say they are rolling out physical infrastructure tweaks, like clearer on-property wayfinding and custom in-app guidance designed to make pickups and drop-offs actually work smoothly for driverless cars.
Uber’s playbook of welcoming a variety of small and large robotaxi players into its app came after the company pivoted away from building its own self-driving tech.
Unlike Uber’s human drivers, Zoox has some geographic limitations.
Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana recently announced an end to her company’s exclusive partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta by January 2028, calling it a “crapshoot.”
To keep Zoox’s pods from getting stuck in endless resort traffic loops, the partnership goes beyond simple branding.

Just like with Uber’s other AV partnerships (like Waymo in Phoenix and Austin, for now), riders can toggle a preference in the app’s Ride Preferences settings to boost their chances of getting an autonomous pod.
Of course, Uber’s strategy has had some drawbacks, too.
The company’s robotaxis only cover heavy tourist zones, like the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, and the Arts District.

coreStoryFacts.text: Amazon 's Zoox is making its toaster-shaped self-driving vehicles available through the Uber app in Las Vegas starting this summer, the latest sign of momentum in the nascent but fast-growing robotaxi market.
"This partnership is an opportunity to continue advancing the use of autonomous mobility in daily life," Zoox CEO Aicha Evans said in a statement.
"Through our collaboration, Zoox will provide a differentiated rider experience to those who already know and love the convenience of riding with Uber."
Amazon, which acquired Zoox in 2020, is way behind Alphabet's Waymo, the U.S. robotaxi leader.
Waymo said in February that it had surpassed 400,000 weekly rides across six U.S. metro areas.
It's now operating its service commercially in 10 U.S. cities, and aiming for expansion to London and Tokyo in 2026.
Zoox began offering free driverless rides last year around the Las Vegas Strip and certain San Francisco neighborhoods.
While it's served more than 300,000 riders, the company said in early March it's not yet offering paid rides.
Earlier this week, Zoox announced an expansion of its testing efforts across some cities in the South.

During Uber's fourth-quarter earnings call in February, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told analysts that AVs available via his company's app attain "significantly higher utilization" than robotaxis hailed on "stand-alone platforms," basing those estimates on unspecified publicly available data.
Trips per AV, per day are 30% higher on Uber, Khosrowshahi said.
As first-party robotaxi brand services and apps become more familiar to travelers and commuters, they could take market share away from Uber and rivals like Lyft or DiDi in China.
Zoox is seeking an exemption from U.S. regulators to commercially deploy its robotaxis.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Tuesday opened up public comments on Zoox's petition, which seeks permission to operate up to 2,500 vehicles on U.S. roads.
As part of a multiyear partnership announced Wednesday, the companies said they plan to make Zoox rides available in Los Angeles next year.
In both cities, Zoox will continue to offer rides on its own app as well.
The Zoox robotaxis have been nicknamed "toasters" due to their shape, with a low step, doors that automatically open and close, and seats that face each other.
Regulators previously gave approval for Zoox to deploy its custom-built vehicles for research and demonstration purposes only.
For Uber, the alliance comes as executives pitch the company's platform as the best way for autonomous vehicle makers to tap rider demand.
Zoox plans to launch initial standalone operations in LA through its own app before the end of 2026, followed by a full Uber integration sometime in 2027.
Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a new robotaxi BFF: Amazon.
Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis.

It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app.
Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge.

During Uber's fourth-quarter earnings call in February, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told analysts that AVs available via his company's app attain "significantly higher utilization" than robotaxis hailed on "stand-alone platforms," basing those estimates on unspecified publicly available data. Trips per AV, per day are 30% higher on Uber, Khosrowshahi said.

By the end of 2026, Uber is aiming to offer driverless rides in 15 cities, the company said in a statement. It already has driverless options in Atlanta, Austin, Texas, Dallas and Phoenix in the U.S., and in several Middle East cities with a variety of partners.
As first-party robotaxi brand services and apps become more familiar to travelers and commuters, they could take market share away from Uber and rivals like Lyft or DiDi in China.
Tesla has launched a Robotaxi-branded app and ride-sharing service, and has begun testing a small number of driverless vehicles in Austin in its fleet.

Zoox began offering free driverless rides last year around the Las Vegas Strip and certain San Francisco neighborhoods. While it's served more than 300,000 riders, the company said in early March it's not yet offering paid rides. Earlier this week, Zoox announced an expansion of its testing efforts across some cities in the South.

The Zoox robotaxis have been nicknamed "toasters" due to their shape, with a low step, doors that automatically open and close, and seats that face each other. The vehicles have a top speed of 75 mph but typically operate at or below 45 mph.

Zoox is seeking an exemption from U.S. regulators to commercially deploy its robotaxis. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Tuesday opened up public comments on Zoox's petition, which seeks permission to operate up to 2,500 vehicles on U.S. roads.
Regulators previously gave approval for Zoox to deploy its custom-built vehicles for research and demonstration purposes only.

passages: Zoox plans to launch initial standalone operations in LA through its own app before the end of 2026, followed by a full Uber integration sometime in 2027.
Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a new robotaxi BFF: Amazon.
Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis.

It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app.
Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge.

MGM, Uber, and Zoox say they are rolling out physical infrastructure tweaks, like clearer on-property wayfinding and custom in-app guidance designed to make pickups and drop-offs actually work smoothly for driverless cars.

Unlike Uber’s human drivers, Zoox has some geographic limitations.
Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana recently announced an end to her company’s exclusive partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta by January 2028, calling it a “crapshoot.”
To keep Zoox’s pods from getting stuck in endless resort traffic loops, the partnership goes beyond simple branding.

Just like with Uber’s other AV partnerships (like Waymo in Phoenix and Austin, for now), riders can toggle a preference in the app’s Ride Preferences settings to boost their chances of getting an autonomous pod.
Of course, Uber’s strategy has had some drawbacks, too.
The company’s robotaxis only cover heavy tourist zones, like the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, and the Arts District.

sources.title: Zoox robotaxis are now on the Uber app in Las Vegas
passages: Zoox robotaxis are officially available through the Uber app in Las Vegas, marking the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company’s first partnership with a third-party ride-hailing platform.
The partnership is expected to extend beyond Las Vegas.

Zoox will begin initial robotaxi operations in Los Angeles this year (introducing the robotaxi and opening rides to Zoox employees, family, and friends), but commercial service will not begin until 2027.

Earlier this year, the Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved a permit that allowed Uber to deploy up to 1,000 robotaxis in Clark County — home to Las Vegas — through its partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox.
Customers won’t be able to select a Zoox robotaxi — at least initially.
Instead, people who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save ride may be matched with one of Zoox’s custom-built robotaxis once they hail a ride.
Uber and Zoox said they’ll work with MGM Resorts to improve pickup and drop-off locations, along with signage to help riders navigate sprawling MGM properties and find the robotaxis.
The launch on Monday is a milestone for both companies.
Uber gets to add another partner to its app as part of its broader strategy to become the primary purveyor of autonomous vehicle technology in North America, Europe, and the Middle East.
That exclusive partnership, which matches Waymo robotaxis with Uber riders in Austin and Atlanta, will end in January 2028.
Waymo plans to offer its rides directly through its own smartphone app as it does in other cities.
For Zoox, the partnership and launch gives it access to more potential customers who might otherwise not try its robotaxi, a needed boost as it trails market leaders Tesla and Waymo.

The two companies also announced a multi-year partnership with MGM Resorts International: they’re rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts properties in Las Vegas. TechCrunch previously confirmed with Uber that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree. And unlike its partnership with other AV developers, Uber told TechCrunch that it will not provide maintenance and other services for Zoox in the Las Vegas market.

US vehicle safety rules were written assuming a human driver sits behind a wheel. passages: Uber riders in Las Vegas can now be matched with a robotaxi that has no steering wheel, no pedals and no front seat. The vehicle comes from Zoox, the autonomous driving company owned by Amazon .
Two companies that compete for your wallet in plenty of other places are now sharing a car.

The integration breaks new ground for each company. It is the first time Uber has put a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle on its network. It is also the first time Zoox has opened its fleet to an outside app.
Until now, if you wanted to ride in a Zoox, you went through Zoox. Now you can get one without ever downloading its app.
Uber says riders who order an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric or Wait & Save trip in Las Vegas may be paired with a Zoox. The pairing carries no extra charge.
Zoox will keep running its own dedicated app alongside the Uber integration. Riders get two front doors to the same vehicle.
Most robotaxis on US roads today are regular cars retrofitted with sensors and software. Zoox took a different route. Its vehicle was designed from scratch for autonomous driving.
The robotaxi seats four passengers who face each other. There is no steering wheel and no pedals, and the vehicle is bidirectional, meaning it can travel either way without needing to turn around.

US vehicle safety rules were written assuming a human driver sits behind a wheel. Zoox’s vehicle became the first purpose-built autonomous vehicle approved for paid rides in the US, via an exemption from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). Paid service in Las Vegas began on August 10, 2026, after that exemption came through.

Zoox did not arrive in Las Vegas through Uber. It started operating independently in the city with free rides in September 2025. Nearly a year later, in August 2026, it moved to paid trips.
Airport access for Zoox customers started on September 3, 2026. As of November 2026, service hours stretch from 6 a.m. to 3 a.m. daily.

Zoox has also pushed its service area into the Arts District and downtown Las Vegas. The company has a multi-year deal to serve as the official autonomous ride-hail partner of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, starting in 2027.
Roughly 62 Zoox vehicles were reported in operation across Las Vegas and the Bay Area as of mid-November 2026.
Uber and Zoox announced their partnership on March 11, 2026. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi highlighted the importance of the tie-up during the company’s third-quarter earnings call.
The Zoox deal lands while Uber’s arrangement with Waymo is being reshaped. Waymo plans to end its exclusive routing partnership with Uber in certain markets by January 2028.
Waymo’s stated reason is rider demand for a consistent app experience.

Las Vegas is already a crowded robotaxi market. Multiple operators, Waymo included, offer autonomous rides in the city. Uber adding Zoox gives its riders access to one more option without leaving the app they already use.
For Uber, the company doesn’t build its own self-driving cars. It wants to be the place where everyone else’s self-driving cars find customers.
By opening its fleet to a third-party app for the first time, Zoox gains instant access to Uber’s existing rider base in Las Vegas.
A fleet of about 62 vehicles split between two regions means most Uber trips in Las Vegas will still be handled by human drivers. The pairing is a possibility, not a promise.
Zoox’s paid service depends on its NHTSA exemption. Any change in how federal regulators treat vehicles without manual controls would directly affect how far this model can scale.
The Grand Prix deal starting in 2027 will be a visible stress test. Major events bring crowds, road closures and heavy demand.

story.title: Zoox robotaxis are now on the Uber app in Las Vegas

facts.text: Amazon 's Zoox is making its toaster-shaped self-driving vehicles available through the Uber app in Las Vegas starting this summer, the latest sign of momentum in the nascent but fast-growing robotaxi market.
"This partnership is an opportunity to continue advancing the use of autonomous mobility in daily life," Zoox CEO Aicha Evans said in a statement.
"Through our collaboration, Zoox will provide a differentiated rider experience to those who already know and love the convenience of riding with Uber."
Amazon, which acquired Zoox in 2020, is way behind Alphabet's Waymo, the U.S. robotaxi leader.
Waymo said in February that it had surpassed 400,000 weekly rides across six U.S. metro areas.
It's now operating its service commercially in 10 U.S. cities, and aiming for expansion to London and Tokyo in 2026.
Zoox began offering free driverless rides last year around the Las Vegas Strip and certain San Francisco neighborhoods.
While it's served more than 300,000 riders, the company said in early March it's not yet offering paid rides.
Earlier this week, Zoox announced an expansion of its testing efforts across some cities in the South.

During Uber's fourth-quarter earnings call in February, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told analysts that AVs available via his company's app attain "significantly higher utilization" than robotaxis hailed on "stand-alone platforms," basing those estimates on unspecified publicly available data.
Trips per AV, per day are 30% higher on Uber, Khosrowshahi said.
As first-party robotaxi brand services and apps become more familiar to travelers and commuters, they could take market share away from Uber and rivals like Lyft or DiDi in China.
Zoox is seeking an exemption from U.S. regulators to commercially deploy its robotaxis.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Tuesday opened up public comments on Zoox's petition, which seeks permission to operate up to 2,500 vehicles on U.S. roads.
As part of a multiyear partnership announced Wednesday, the companies said they plan to make Zoox rides available in Los Angeles next year.
In both cities, Zoox will continue to offer rides on its own app as well.
The Zoox robotaxis have been nicknamed "toasters" due to their shape, with a low step, doors that automatically open and close, and seats that face each other.
Regulators previously gave approval for Zoox to deploy its custom-built vehicles for research and demonstration purposes only.
For Uber, the alliance comes as executives pitch the company's platform as the best way for autonomous vehicle makers to tap rider demand.
Zoox plans to launch initial standalone operations in LA through its own app before the end of 2026, followed by a full Uber integration sometime in 2027.
Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a new robotaxi BFF: Amazon.
Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis.

It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app.
Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge.

MGM, Uber, and Zoox say they are rolling out physical infrastructure tweaks, like clearer on-property wayfinding and custom in-app guidance designed to make pickups and drop-offs actually work smoothly for driverless cars.
Uber’s playbook of welcoming a variety of small and large robotaxi players into its app came after the company pivoted away from building its own self-driving tech.
Unlike Uber’s human drivers, Zoox has some geographic limitations.
Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana recently announced an end to her company’s exclusive partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta by January 2028, calling it a “crapshoot.”
To keep Zoox’s pods from getting stuck in endless resort traffic loops, the partnership goes beyond simple branding.

Just like with Uber’s other AV partnerships (like Waymo in Phoenix and Austin, for now), riders can toggle a preference in the app’s Ride Preferences settings to boost their chances of getting an autonomous pod.
Of course, Uber’s strategy has had some drawbacks, too.
The company’s robotaxis only cover heavy tourist zones, like the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, and the Arts District.
Zoox robotaxis are officially available through the Uber app in Las Vegas, marking the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company’s first partnership with a third-party ride-hailing platform.
The partnership is expected to extend beyond Las Vegas.

Zoox will begin initial robotaxi operations in Los Angeles this year (introducing the robotaxi and opening rides to Zoox employees, family, and friends), but commercial service will not begin until 2027.

Earlier this year, the Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved a permit that allowed Uber to deploy up to 1,000 robotaxis in Clark County — home to Las Vegas — through its partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox.
Customers won’t be able to select a Zoox robotaxi — at least initially.
Instead, people who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save ride may be matched with one of Zoox’s custom-built robotaxis once they hail a ride.
Uber and Zoox said they’ll work with MGM Resorts to improve pickup and drop-off locations, along with signage to help riders navigate sprawling MGM properties and find the robotaxis.
The launch on Monday is a milestone for both companies.
Uber gets to add another partner to its app as part of its broader strategy to become the primary purveyor of autonomous vehicle technology in North America, Europe, and the Middle East.
That exclusive partnership, which matches Waymo robotaxis with Uber riders in Austin and Atlanta, will end in January 2028.
Waymo plans to offer its rides directly through its own smartphone app as it does in other cities.
For Zoox, the partnership and launch gives it access to more potential customers who might otherwise not try its robotaxi, a needed boost as it trails market leaders Tesla and Waymo.

sources.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy - BBC
passages: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang.

Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.
