Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.

Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.

And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.

But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.
Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.

I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.

I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.

Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.

Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.

Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.

People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.
Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?

Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

extraction.body: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) had enough to deal with on Wednesday night. The Wall Street Journal reported at 5:27 PM ET that its board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang and could meet as soon as Wednesday, hours after a New York Times report that Huang had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has not commented. The same day, its biggest customer laid out a long-term plan that runs through Nvidia’s profit margin. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told about 50 presidents of Samsung companies that OpenAI’s edge will come from owning the whole stack. Asked whether heavy spending was squeezing returns, Altman said “that’s the point”: a company with “vertically integrated infrastructure that costs less than any other company’s” can sell AI in huge volume at thin margins and pull ahead of the competition, according to Q&A materials from the October 31 meeting obtained by Korea’s Financial News and published Wednesday. The article says OpenAI’s investments in efficiency, including chips it designs itself, are starting to pay off. Read plainly, that is a plan to stop paying Nvidia’s prices. Nvidia sells the most expensive layer of AI infrastructure at some of the widest margins in the industry. A customer whose strategy is to run that infrastructure cheaper than anyone else has to replace that layer with its own over the medium to long term. Nvidia was at $160.03 in after-hours trading at 7:15 PM ET, down 7.9% from Wednesday’s close, 14.3% below the November 6 close and 33.1% below its October 6 record close. OpenAI has been building toward this for a year. In 2025 it signed a letter of intent with Nvidia for 10 gigawatts of Nvidia systems, with Nvidia planning to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as they were deployed. Within weeks it agreed to buy 6 gigawatts of AMD chips and announced a 10-gigawatt deal with Broadcom to build custom accelerators of OpenAI’s own design, with deployment starting in the second half of 2026. Each step moves more of OpenAI’s computing away from a single supplier, and the Broadcom chips move it onto silicon OpenAI controls. Altman’s remarks to Samsung explain why. Selling AI in high volumes at thin margins only works if the cost of each unit of computing keeps falling, and the fastest way to cut that cost is to stop paying a supplier’s markup. “If we can build vertically integrated infrastructure at a lower cost than anyone else,” as one English translation of his comment circulating on X put it, “we can get ahead of the competition.” Altman made two other points in the same meeting that Nvidia holders will not like. He said “there has been double-counting of demand” for AI, and that “only two companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are actually driving major demand growth.” A boom that rests on two buyers gives those two buyers enormous bargaining power, and one of them has just described a plan to need Nvidia less. He also gave the bull case: “In the long term, AI demand will grow enormously,” and the biggest limit for the next few years is “the chip supply chain and data center infrastructure.” The world is still short of chips, which keeps Nvidia’s sales high for now. The question for a holder is what Nvidia can charge once its largest customers make their own. A holder who had $100,000 in Nvidia at the November 6 close, about 536 shares, has about $85,743 at the after-hours price, a loss of about $14,257 in three trading sessions and an evening. Almost all of that came from the Huang scandal. Altman’s plan is a slower risk: it goes to Nvidia’s gross margin, the number to watch in every quarterly report from here, and it matters more over five years than who is CEO next month. For a holder deciding what to do before Thursday’s open, the practical question is concentration. If Nvidia is more than about 10% of a retirement portfolio, both the board’s decision and OpenAI’s plan land on that one position. Trimming inside an IRA costs nothing in taxes. In a recent appearance on Dwarkesh Podcast, Huang once again said that working with China then 'against China' is in the interests of the US. The day that DeepSeek comes out on Huawei first, that is a horrible outcome for our nation."When asked about how DeepSeek's being an open source model can hurt America's proprietary systems, considering that it can run on any system. You described a situation that I perceive to be good news. A company developed software, developed an AI model, and it runs best on the American tech stack. You set it up as a premise that it was bad news. I’m going to give you the bad news, that AI models around the world are developed and they run best on non-American hardware. That is bad news for us." When asked how shipping chips to China is keeping the US ahead, considering that the bottleneck is on compute. Number one, why is it that we don’t come up with a regulation that’s more balanced so that Nvidia can win around the world instead of giving up the world? Why would you want the United States to give up the world? The chip industry is part of the American ecosystem. Huang replied after constant prodding, "We have to keep innovating and, as you probably know, our share is growing, not decreasing. The fact that I can buy this car brand one day and use another car brand another day, easy. Because I don’t think the United States is a loser.

extraction.body: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here . Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. passages: SpaceX Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder were among more than 158,000 signatories by Sunday demanding Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief pending an independent investigation.

Huang resigned Thursday after revelations of two extramarital affairs, one with a subordinate and another with a woman accused of spying for China, ending his 33-year tenure at the helm of the artificial intelligence giant.

extraction.body: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) had enough to deal with on Wednesday night. The Wall Street Journal reported at 5:27 PM ET that its board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang and could meet as soon as Wednesday, hours after a New York Times report that Huang had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has not commented. The same day, its biggest customer laid out a long-term plan that runs through Nvidia’s profit margin. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told about 50 presidents of Samsung companies that OpenAI’s edge will come from owning the whole stack. Asked whether heavy spending was squeezing returns, Altman said “that’s the point”: a company with “vertically integrated infrastructure that costs less than any other company’s” can sell AI in huge volume at thin margins and pull ahead of the competition, according to Q&A materials from the October 31 meeting obtained by Korea’s Financial News and published Wednesday. The article says OpenAI’s investments in efficiency, including chips it designs itself, are starting to pay off. Read plainly, that is a plan to stop paying Nvidia’s prices. Nvidia sells the most expensive layer of AI infrastructure at some of the widest margins in the industry. A customer whose strategy is to run that infrastructure cheaper than anyone else has to replace that layer with its own over the medium to long term. Nvidia was at $160.03 in after-hours trading at 7:15 PM ET, down 7.9% from Wednesday’s close, 14.3% below the November 6 close and 33.1% below its October 6 record close. OpenAI has been building toward this for a year. In 2025 it signed a letter of intent with Nvidia for 10 gigawatts of Nvidia systems, with Nvidia planning to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as they were deployed. Within weeks it agreed to buy 6 gigawatts of AMD chips and announced a 10-gigawatt deal with Broadcom to build custom accelerators of OpenAI’s own design, with deployment starting in the second half of 2026. Each step moves more of OpenAI’s computing away from a single supplier, and the Broadcom chips move it onto silicon OpenAI controls. Altman’s remarks to Samsung explain why. Selling AI in high volumes at thin margins only works if the cost of each unit of computing keeps falling, and the fastest way to cut that cost is to stop paying a supplier’s markup. “If we can build vertically integrated infrastructure at a lower cost than anyone else,” as one English translation of his comment circulating on X put it, “we can get ahead of the competition.” Altman made two other points in the same meeting that Nvidia holders will not like. He said “there has been double-counting of demand” for AI, and that “only two companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are actually driving major demand growth.” A boom that rests on two buyers gives those two buyers enormous bargaining power, and one of them has just described a plan to need Nvidia less. He also gave the bull case: “In the long term, AI demand will grow enormously,” and the biggest limit for the next few years is “the chip supply chain and data center infrastructure.” The world is still short of chips, which keeps Nvidia’s sales high for now. The question for a holder is what Nvidia can charge once its largest customers make their own. A holder who had $100,000 in Nvidia at the November 6 close, about 536 shares, has about $85,743 at the after-hours price, a loss of about $14,257 in three trading sessions and an evening. Almost all of that came from the Huang scandal. Altman’s plan is a slower risk: it goes to Nvidia’s gross margin, the number to watch in every quarterly report from here, and it matters more over five years than who is CEO next month. For a holder deciding what to do before Thursday’s open, the practical question is concentration. If Nvidia is more than about 10% of a retirement portfolio, both the board’s decision and OpenAI’s plan land on that one position. Trimming inside an IRA costs nothing in taxes. Trimming in a taxable account turns part of the gain into a tax bill, which is worth knowing before selling on a night like this. Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections. Selling AI in high volumes at thin margins only works if the cost of each unit of computing keeps falling, and the fastest way to cut that cost is to stop paying a supplier’s markup. “If we can build vertically integrated infrastructure at a lower cost than anyone else,” as one English translation of his comment circulating on X put it, “we can get ahead of the competition.”

Altman made two other points in the same meeting that Nvidia holders will not like. He said “there has been double-counting of demand” for AI, and that “only two companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are actually driving major demand growth.” A boom that rests on two buyers gives those two buyers enormous bargaining power, and one of them has just described a plan to need Nvidia less.

He also gave the bull case: “In the long term, AI demand will grow enormously,” and the biggest limit for the next few years is “the chip supply chain and data center infrastructure.” The world is still short of chips, which keeps Nvidia’s sales high for now. The question for a holder is what Nvidia can charge once its largest customers make their own.

A holder who had $100,000 in Nvidia at the November 6 close, about 536 shares, has about $85,743 at the after-hours price, a loss of about $14,257 in three trading sessions and an evening. Almost all of that came from the Huang scandal. Altman’s plan is a slower risk: it goes to Nvidia’s gross margin, the number to watch in every quarterly report from here, and it matters more over five years than who is CEO next month.

For a holder deciding what to do before Thursday’s open, the practical question is concentration. If Nvidia is more than about 10% of a retirement portfolio, both the board’s decision and OpenAI’s plan land on that one position. Trimming inside an IRA costs nothing in taxes. Trimming in a taxable account turns part of the gain into a tax bill, which is worth knowing before selling on a night like this.

extraction.body: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months. The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week . passages: Apple and clinical AI platform OpenEvidence want up to 200,000 US participants to ask health questions and grade the answers
Sun 15 Nov 2026 · 20:30 EST · 3 min read
Apple wants to know whether AI health answers are actually any good. Rather than guess, it is asking up to 200,000 people to grade them.

The company announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, 2026, in partnership with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform built for healthcare professionals. Participants will use a dedicated iOS app to ask medical questions, then score the responses on accuracy, detail and relevance.
The study is virtual and limited to the US. Eligible participants must be 21 or older, and enrollment opened the same day as the announcement, with the app already available to download.

Once inside the app, users type in health questions the way they might ask a friend who went to medical school. The answers come from OpenEvidence, which grounds its responses in peer-reviewed literature, including The New England Journal of Medicine , JAMA and Nature.
After each answer, participants rate what they received. The research focuses on four areas: user trust, response quality, comprehension, and the effect on health decision-making.
Participants control their survey responses, and privacy protections apply throughout the study.

The study departs from Apple’s earlier health research, which centered on data collected by its devices. The Apple Health Study, which began in February 2025, is one example of that device-first approach.

OpenEvidence may not be a household name, but it has become a fixture in many clinicians’ workflows. Its user base among monthly active US clinicians grew from 355 in January 2024 to 703,265 by June 2026.
The platform has also handled 271 million queries over 30 months.
OpenEvidence reached a valuation of approximately $15 billion after a $250 million funding round in September 2026.
The company has also integrated with major US health systems, pushing clinical AI deeper into everyday hospital operations.
The launch comes as scrutiny of AI in healthcare intensifies. In mid-October 2026, JAMA published a comprehensive analysis of how clinicians use these tools, adding fuel to an already active debate.

For Apple, the study offers something valuable: large-scale, structured feedback on how people engage with health AI before committing to a consumer product. With up to 200,000 participants, the dataset could give the company a clearer picture of where these tools earn trust and where they lose it.
The stated goal is to improve conversational health AI design for Apple and for the wider healthcare industry.
The study’s focus on comprehension suggests both companies are aware that translating medical literature for laypeople without distorting it is a hard design problem.

Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months. The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week . Sun 15 Nov 2026 · 20:30 EST · 3 min read
Apple wants to know whether AI health answers are actually any good. Rather than guess, it is asking up to 200,000 people to grade them.

The company announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, 2026, in partnership with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform built for healthcare professionals. Participants will use a dedicated iOS app to ask medical questions, then score the responses on accuracy, detail and relevance.
The study is virtual and limited to the US. Eligible participants must be 21 or older, and enrollment opened the same day as the announcement, with the app already available to download.

Once inside the app, users type in health questions the way they might ask a friend who went to medical school. The answers come from OpenEvidence, which grounds its responses in peer-reviewed literature, including The New England Journal of Medicine , JAMA and Nature.
After each answer, participants rate what they received. The research focuses on four areas: user trust, response quality, comprehension, and the effect on health decision-making.
Participants control their survey responses, and privacy protections apply throughout the study.

The study departs from Apple’s earlier health research, which centered on data collected by its devices. The Apple Health Study, which began in February 2025, is one example of that device-first approach.

story.title: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health

facts.text: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features.
Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health.
But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding.
Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled.
The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.
The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users.
It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet.
Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models.
The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

It draws medical information from established scientific publications, including The New England Journal of Medicine.How many participants is Apple looking for?Apple aims to recruit up to 200,000 participants for its Health AI Usage Study.Who is eligible for Apple's AI health study?The study is currently open to people who live in the United States, are at least 21 years old, and own an iPhone 15 Pro or newer running iOS 26 or later.Does the Apple Health AI study require access to HealthKit data?No.

Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

Participants will also be asked to complete regular surveys to help researchers better understand how AI-generated health information is interpreted and used.Apple targets up to 200,000 participantsApple is planning to enrol around 2,00,000 adults in the United States for the virtual study.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”Dedicated app allows users to ask health questionsAs part of the initiative, Apple has released a dedicated iOS app that lets participants ask health-related questions and receive responses grounded in clinical research.
Apple stresses that the app isn’t meant to diagnose or treat any condition or replace a medical professional’s advice.Your child uses AI every day.
Answers are supported by peer-reviewed medical sources, including publications such as The New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA and Nature, according to Apple and OpenEvidence.

extraction.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's spy-sex scandal . But the Commerce Department is in charge "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's " Squawk Box ." The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed. Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported. Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room. Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room." But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s." "And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy. Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales. Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down." "The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" "I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said. The Commerce Department did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Bessent's remarks. Huang and Lutnick both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Thursday . Eichamer, the Commerce spokeswoman, told CNBC on Friday that Lutnick "has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions." Huang has separately been asked to sit for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 before the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs. The Republican chairmen of those panels have also asked Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to participate in a closed-door interview with them on Dec. 2. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., separately asked Jeff Kessler, Commerce's under secretary for industry and security, to appear before his committee on Dec. 3 for a hearing on "chip smuggling, adversary military use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations." sources.title: Senator slams Commerce Secretary for flow of Nvidia AI chips to China
passages: Washington Senator Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia’s AI chips away from China.

The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for Commerce Secretary.

While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a new initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals.

Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries.
The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

extraction.body: Washington Senator Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia’s AI chips away from China. In a letter to Lutnick on Sunday, Cantwell said the DOC has “undermined America’s national security,” and that its failures “help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.” > “Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology.” In her letter, Cantwell specifically calls out instances when the DOC reportedly didn’t heed warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed’s access to AI chips, prior to allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a then-Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy. Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries. The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for Commerce Secretary. The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a new initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals.

Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries.
The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

extraction.body: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, accused the Commerce Department in a letter to Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday, Nov. 15, of failing to stop advanced U.S. AI chips from reaching China, CNBC and The Verge reported [1] [2] . "Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People's Republic of China (PRC)," she wrote, adding that "these failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI" [1] [2] . Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving them [1] . She sent the letter ahead of President Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Thursday, Nov. 19 [1] [2] . The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Monday [1] . According to The Verge, the letter says Commerce did not act on warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed's access to AI chips before reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive U.S. officials suspect of passing information to China [2] . Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 . Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last week that the Megaspeed blacklisting stalled because Commerce "has the pen" . Cantwell also criticized Commerce for letting Alibaba and ByteDance use Nvidia chips through overseas data centers and for extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain U.S. AI technology through subsidiaries, The Verge reported [2] . The New York Times reported on Nov. 15 that Lutnick pushed for narrower rules on overseas data centers serving Chinese customers . On conflicts, Cantwell said Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick led and his sons now control, held $1.2 billion of Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination [1] . She said the administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology" [1] . "America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," she wrote [1] . CNBC reported last week that Cantor held 1.81 million Nvidia shares worth $362 million at the end of June. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) has summoned Jensen Huang and Lutnick to testify in December, and Commerce spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said last week that Lutnick has agreed to appear [1] . Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have given Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller until Nov. 17 to confirm they have ordered Nvidia export records preserved [1] . Lawmakers in both parties are also moving toward tighter AI chip export rules . "The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America's most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries," Cantwell wrote in closing [2] . Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that the administration plans to name Nvidia and other U.S. AI companies "national champions" to help them expand overseas. extraction.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's spy-sex scandal . But the Commerce Department is in charge "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's " Squawk Box ." The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed. Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported. Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room. Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room." But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s." "And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy. Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales. Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down." "The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" "I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said. The Commerce Department did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Bessent's remarks. Huang and Lutnick both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Thursday . Eichamer, the Commerce spokeswoman, told CNBC on Friday that Lutnick "has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions." Huang has separately been asked to sit for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 before the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs. The Republican chairmen of those panels have also asked Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to participate in a closed-door interview with them on Dec. 2. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., separately asked Jeff Kessler, Commerce's under secretary for industry and security, to appear before his committee on Dec. 3 for a hearing on "chip smuggling, adversary military use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations." extraction.body: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected. "Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires. Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail. At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data… — vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026 In short, leanPCS is a proposed way for Ethereum to bundle many large, quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a single compact proof, so that the full data never has to be stored onchain. It is built on polynomial commitment schemes, or PCS, the core mathematical building block of STARK proofs. Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today. The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes. "This is unsustainable to put on chain," he wrote. Buterin's answer is EIP-8288, a draft proposal he co-authored with developer Thomas Coratger in June, which would aggregate those signatures and proofs before they ever reach a block. Under the design, users publish their signatures or proofs, and network nodes repeatedly bundle everything they have seen into a single STARK, a type of zero-knowledge proof , that attests the underlying data is valid. These aggregate proofs are themselves combined until a single "master proof" verifies everything in a block. Only short claims, rather than the full signatures or proofs, would need to be stored onchain. He laid out three ways to build it, depending on what users submit. The simplest, leanSPHINCS, would support a single type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature, costing users only a small amount of gas per signature, but it couldn't do anything else. At the other end, leanSTARK would be fully general, allowing any signature scheme, privacy protocols or hidden multisig logic. But Ethereum would first have to agree on a programming language for users' programs, which Buterin called "the first big case of 'Ethereum moving beyond the EVM,'" and which is likely to take time. Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route. It would offer the same generality as leanSTARK but "could potentially be implemented very quickly," he said, because far fewer design choices are needed, and leanSTARK could then be added later. "So there is a route to getting 'the cryptographic proof singularity' much faster than any of us expected," Buterin wrote, "and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS." Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers. The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate. Under protocol-level aggregation, a future "leanSPHINCS" verification would cost about 3,000 gas, according to the post. Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated post-quantum team in January, and Buterin has since said the network is betting its future on quantum security and privacy. Developers have also proposed overhauling the staking deposit contract to support post-quantum validator keys, and Buterin has pushed a plan to cut the cost of quantum-safe privacy. How we work Vitalik Buterin has reversed his view on leanPCS , backing it as a potentially faster route to a quantum-safe Ethereum upgrade. Buterin favors leanPCS because it promises broad cryptographic flexibility with fewer implementation decisions than leanSTARK. His endorsement marks a sharp change in his assessment. “Over the past few weeks I’ve gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull,” Buterin wrote. The security problem behind the proposal extends beyond Ethereum . Quantum computers are expected eventually to break the elliptic curve cryptography currently protecting Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts. It would handle one type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature at a small gas cost per signature, but would not support other uses. leanSTARK would support any signature scheme, privacy protocols, and hidden multisignature logic. That flexibility comes with a prerequisite: Ethereum would first need to agree on a programming language for users’ programs, moving beyond the Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM. Buterin said that process would likely take time. By contrast, he said leanPCS “could potentially be implemented very quickly,” with leanSTARK added later. Vitalik Buterin has reversed his view on leanPCS , backing it as a potentially faster route to a quantum-safe Ethereum upgrade. In a November 16, 2026 post, Buterin supported a proposal that would compress bulky quantum-resistant signatures and proofs rather than store their full data onchain.
Buterin favors leanPCS because it promises broad cryptographic flexibility with fewer implementation decisions than leanSTARK.
His endorsement marks a sharp change in his assessment.
“Over the past few weeks I’ve gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull,” Buterin wrote.

The security problem behind the proposal extends beyond Ethereum . Quantum computers are expected eventually to break the elliptic curve cryptography currently protecting Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts. Quantum-resistant replacements address that threat, but their much larger signatures and proofs create storage and gas-cost challenges.
Buterin’s explainer focuses on handling that extra data through aggregation: verifying many signatures and proofs together, without requiring Ethereum to retain all of them onchain.

leanPCS uses polynomial commitment schemes , or PCS—the mathematical foundation of STARK proofs—to bundle large quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a compact proof. Buterin described it as an approach that offers leanSTARK’s generality while requiring fewer design choices.
The three proposed approaches differ in what users would be able to submit and how much development work they require.
leanSPHINCS is the simplest option. It would handle one type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature at a small gas cost per signature, but would not support other uses.

leanSTARK would support any signature scheme, privacy protocols, and hidden multisignature logic. That flexibility comes with a prerequisite: Ethereum would first need to agree on a programming language for users’ programs, moving beyond the Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM. Buterin said that process would likely take time.

By contrast, he said leanPCS “could potentially be implemented very quickly,” with leanSTARK added later. That is the implementation advantage behind his support for leanPCS as a route toward a quantum-safe Ethereum upgrade.

According to Buterin’s explainer, moving to quantum-safe cryptography would push signature sizes up from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes , while zero-knowledge proofs would expand from just a few hundred bytes to roughly 128 kilobytes .
“This is unsustainable to put on chain,” he wrote.

In the proposed aggregation scheme, users submit signatures or proofs, and nodes throughout the network continually merge the data they’ve received into STARK proofs certifying its validity. These aggregate proofs are then merged again and again until a single master proof confirms everything contained in a block.
Rather than storing all of the underlying data, Ethereum would keep only brief claims backed by the aggregate proof.

Buterin additionally highlighted SPHINCS- , a hash-based signature family tailored for Ethereum. Shared on the Ethereum Research forum in June with contributions from Buterin and cryptographers at the Ethereum Foundation, the work shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can be verified without any changes to the protocol.
The verification costs about 150,000 gas , the research post shows, compared with approximately 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature under an earlier Buterin estimate.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has backed a faster route toward quantum-safe wallets using leanPCS, a method designed to aggregate large post-quantum signatures and cryptographic checks before they are permanently stored onchain. In a post on X , Buterin said he had shifted from skepticism to strong support for the approach. Standard Ethereum signatures occupy about 65 bytes, while some quantum-resistant alternatives can require roughly 1,000 to 6,000 bytes. The proposal aims to protect Ethereum without forcing every transaction to carry the full data cost of quantum-safe signatures.
Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.
At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data…
— vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026

Under the proposed design, wallets would still generate signatures proving that users authorized transactions, but network participants could combine those signatures with other cryptographic proofs before inclusion in a block. Those batches could then be aggregated again until Ethereum stores one shared proof confirming that all underlying checks passed. The payment instructions and enough verification data would remain onchain, while the bulky individual signatures would not. The model builds on EIP-8288’s recursive aggregation framework , reducing the storage burden created by larger post-quantum authentication schemes.

Buterin now favors leanPCS because it could deliver much of that functionality sooner without requiring Ethereum developers to first standardize a broader computing language for every proof system the network may need to verify. Such a language could provide greater generality, but Buterin described that architectural choice as difficult to reverse once adopted. LeanPCS instead standardizes a narrower mathematical verification tool while allowing developers more flexibility around the systems built above it. That tradeoff could accelerate the 2027 post-quantum push proposed by Ethlabs while accepting somewhat more onchain data than the broader alternative.

The approach could also benefit privacy applications, whose proofs can become significantly larger under stronger cryptographic assumptions. Aggregating those proofs could make advanced privacy and quantum-resistant authorization more practical without making each user pay for the full size of every proof. However, the proposal is not scheduled for activation. EIP-8288 remains a draft, its reference implementation is unfinished, and Buterin’s latest endorsement establishes no mainnet launch date. The faster route therefore strengthens Ethereum’s research direction rather than confirming deployment , complementing other accelerated targets such as the proposed December 2028 post-quantum transition discussed by researcher Justin Drake. It also aligns with recent calls to prioritize quantum defenses over faster block times in Ethereum’s near-term development agenda.

extraction.body: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected. "Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires. Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail. At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data… — vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026 In short, leanPCS is a proposed way for Ethereum to bundle many large, quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a single compact proof, so that the full data never has to be stored onchain. It is built on polynomial commitment schemes, or PCS, the core mathematical building block of STARK proofs. Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today. The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes. "This is unsustainable to put on chain," he wrote. Buterin's answer is EIP-8288, a draft proposal he co-authored with developer Thomas Coratger in June, which would aggregate those signatures and proofs before they ever reach a block. Under the design, users publish their signatures or proofs, and network nodes repeatedly bundle everything they have seen into a single STARK, a type of zero-knowledge proof , that attests the underlying data is valid. These aggregate proofs are themselves combined until a single "master proof" verifies everything in a block. Only short claims, rather than the full signatures or proofs, would need to be stored onchain. He laid out three ways to build it, depending on what users submit. The simplest, leanSPHINCS, would support a single type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature, costing users only a small amount of gas per signature, but it couldn't do anything else. At the other end, leanSTARK would be fully general, allowing any signature scheme, privacy protocols or hidden multisig logic. But Ethereum would first have to agree on a programming language for users' programs, which Buterin called "the first big case of 'Ethereum moving beyond the EVM,'" and which is likely to take time. Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route. It would offer the same generality as leanSTARK but "could potentially be implemented very quickly," he said, because far fewer design choices are needed, and leanSTARK could then be added later. "So there is a route to getting 'the cryptographic proof singularity' much faster than any of us expected," Buterin wrote, "and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS." Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers. The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate. Under protocol-level aggregation, a future "leanSPHINCS" verification would cost about 3,000 gas, according to the post. Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated post-quantum team in January, and Buterin has since said the network is betting its future on quantum security and privacy. Developers have also proposed overhauling the staking deposit contract to support post-quantum validator keys, and Buterin has pushed a plan to cut the cost of quantum-safe privacy. Buterin favors leanPCS because it promises broad cryptographic flexibility with fewer implementation decisions than leanSTARK.
His endorsement marks a sharp change in his assessment.
“Over the past few weeks I’ve gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull,” Buterin wrote.

The security problem behind the proposal extends beyond Ethereum . Quantum computers are expected eventually to break the elliptic curve cryptography currently protecting Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts. Quantum-resistant replacements address that threat, but their much larger signatures and proofs create storage and gas-cost challenges.
Buterin’s explainer focuses on handling that extra data through aggregation: verifying many signatures and proofs together, without requiring Ethereum to retain all of them onchain.

The three proposed approaches differ in what users would be able to submit and how much development work they require.

By contrast, he said leanPCS “could potentially be implemented very quickly,” with leanSTARK added later. That is the implementation advantage behind his support for leanPCS as a route toward a quantum-safe Ethereum upgrade.

Rather than storing all of the underlying data, Ethereum would keep only brief claims backed by the aggregate proof.

Buterin additionally highlighted SPHINCS- , a hash-based signature family tailored for Ethereum. Shared on the Ethereum Research forum in June with contributions from Buterin and cryptographers at the Ethereum Foundation, the work shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can be verified without any changes to the protocol.

facts.text: "Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires.
Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected.
Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today.

The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes.

Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers.

The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate.
Quantum resistance has become a top priority for Ethereum.
Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route.

extraction.body: Jordanian authorities said on Monday that they will block the Telegram social media app in the kingdom over national security concerns.Jordanian Telegram users reported disruptions on Monday, according to Jordanian news outlet Roya News. Shortly after, Jordan's Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced it had blocked the messaging app nationwide.Telegram, a Dubai-based cloud messaging app for mobile and desktop, describes itself on its website as focused on security and speed. It supports end-to-end encrypted chats with self-destruct timers for sensitive messages.Jordan cites crime, extremismThe PSD said the move was meant to stop the platform from being used for cybercrime, threats, extortion, and the spread of illegal content, including extremist material, according to the Jordanian state news agency Petra.The decision comes after a rare deadly church attack last month killed nine people and prompted airstrikes on neighboring Syria that Jordan said killed 20 Islamic State terrorists. On November 5, Jordan said one security officer had been killed and another wounded in what it called a terrorist stabbing attack in Amman.Blocking Telegram is one of several measures aimed specifically at combating Islamist terrorism, Prof. Ronen Yitzhak, an expert on Jordan and head of Bar-Ilan University's Department of Multidisciplinary Studies in the Humanities, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.Jordan has intensified its war on terror, Yitzhak said, not only through counterterrorism operations, such as strikes on Islamic State strongholds in southern Syria, but also by taking the fight to social media. The move is also meant to give Jordanian citizens a renewed sense of security, he added.Barak Gonen, a cybersecurity expert and lecturer at the Jerusalem College of Technology, was more skeptical. Blocking Telegram because it was presumably used to facilitate terrorist attacks is “equivalent [to] stopping all the train transportation in the country because some terrorists are known to be on a train,” he told the Post on Monday.The move is legitimate, Gonen said, but “very extreme.”“I certainly do hope that in [Israel, the Shin Bet] has the capabilities of stopping the specific train without stopping all of the train activity in the country,” he said.Directorate encourages parents to monitor children's online activityBlocking the Telegram app aligns with Jordan's existing legislation to "protect society from the risks associated with the misuse of digital platforms," the PSD claimed, according to Petra.The directorate also urged citizens to use social media with caution, avoid interacting with suspicious accounts or unknown users, and report illegal activity. It called on parents to monitor their children's internet use, use parental controls on internet-connected devices, and “encourage safe and responsible use of technology.”Telegram did not immediately respond to The Jerusalem Post's request for comment. However, the company's automatic reply noted that “Telegram is committed to protecting user privacy and human rights such as freedom of speech and assembly.”Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, is regarded as a relatively stable state in the Middle East. Its security services have foiled plots by Islamist terrorists in the past, including suspected Islamic State supporters.Over the years, Islamic State militants have used the mobile messaging service, created by Pavel Durov, who is in exile from Russia, to issue statements.Durov faces investigations in several countries. In July, Russia said it had ​charged him with facilitating terrorist activity, alleging that his app was being used by ‌Ukrainian spies to organize attacks inside Russia.Durov denies wrongdoing and says Telegram has exceeded its obligations to moderate content and cooperate with authorities to fight crime. Iraq also moves to block TelegramLater on Monday, Iraq's Communications and Media Commission (CMC) announced that Telegram would be blocked across the country, “due to the company's failure to comply with the applicable legal and regulatory requirements.”The move is meant to push the company to review Iraqi content on the app, prevent violations, and cooperate with the commission, the CMC said, as part of wider efforts to curb the use of social media to spread extremism, incite sedition, violence, and hatred, commit cybercrime, and threaten national security.According to the CMC, Telegram did not take adequate action to combat the dissemination of content that violates Iraqi law. The commission gave Telegram a 30-day grace period to rectify the situation, although it did not specify what would happen if Telegram failed to do so.The ban comes six months after the commission lifted a week-long ban on the messaging app in May, after the company complied with the regulator's rules, according to Kurdistan Region-based news channel Rudaw Media Network. The commission had cited national security concerns then as well.The app has found a range of uses in Iraq, including by channels affiliated with pro-Iran armed groups, some of which decried Monday's decision, Rudaw reported.It also comes nearly a month after Iraq's Communications Ministry banned the navigation app Waze, citing the presence of the company's data centers in Israel, Rudaw reported.Reuters contributed to this report.

The PSD urged citizens to “exercise caution when using social media applications,” avoid interacting with accounts, links, or entities of unknown origin, and report unlawful practices or content through official channels. DW said Jordan organised airstrikes on neighbouring Syria and said it had killed 20 so-called "Islamic State" militants, while the government also acknowledged that a number of civilians had been killed in the strikes. Middle East Online said the decision came after the deadly church attack last month killed nine people and prompted airstrikes on neighbouring Syria that Jordan said killed 20 Islamic State militants. The National said nine Christians were killed when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at the St George’s Orthodox Church in Hmoud, about 80km south of Amman, on October 23, and it said the security court sentenced three men to death by hanging after they were convicted of carrying out the attack. Al Jazeera said Russia issued an arrest warrant for Durov in July, accusing him of aiding “terrorism,” and it said he is also being investigated in several other countries. The National said Telegram is used by almost 10 per cent of the Middle East's population, accounting for tens of millions of users, and it said officials did not link the platform to a deadly attack on an Orthodox church last month. 8 outlets in this story. Read their headlines below .

Jordan’s Public Security Directorate announced that Jordan would block the Telegram messaging app in the kingdom over national security concerns tied to “the attempts to spread extremism and radicalisation.” The PSD said the measure aimed to prevent Telegram from being used to facilitate cyber crime, threats and extortion, or to distribute content that violates the law, threatens public security or promotes extremism and radicalism.

The PSD urged citizens to “exercise caution when using social media applications,” avoid interacting with accounts, links, or entities of unknown origin, and report unlawful practices or content through official channels. Jordan’s ban came amid a security crackdown after an attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in the west-central governorate of Karak, and Jordan carried out airstrikes on neighbouring Syria that Amman said killed 20 members of the ISIL (ISIS) armed group linked to the church attack.
Telegram is end-to-end encrypted for some chats

Jordan said a shooting on October 23 at a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Karak governate left seven people dead and another 34 wounded, and a Jordanian court sentenced three men to death by hanging on Sunday in connection with the attack. DW said Jordan organised airstrikes on neighbouring Syria and said it had killed 20 so-called "Islamic State" militants, while the government also acknowledged that a number of civilians had been killed in the strikes.

Middle East Online said the decision came after the deadly church attack last month killed nine people and prompted airstrikes on neighbouring Syria that Jordan said killed 20 Islamic State militants. The National said nine Christians were killed when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at the St George’s Orthodox Church in Hmoud, about 80km south of Amman, on October 23, and it said the security court sentenced three men to death by hanging after they were convicted of carrying out the attack.

Telegram was founded by Russian entrepreneur Pavel Durov in 2013, and Al Jazeera said he is believed to be in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates and faces up to life in a Russian prison if found guilty. Al Jazeera said Russia issued an arrest warrant for Durov in July, accusing him of aiding “terrorism,” and it said he is also being investigated in several other countries.

The National said Telegram is used by almost 10 per cent of the Middle East's population, accounting for tens of millions of users, and it said officials did not link the platform to a deadly attack on an Orthodox church last month. DW said Durov built Telegram with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013, and it said Durov rejects the allegations, arguing that Telegram has gone "beyond its obligations in moderating content and assisting authorities in tackling crime."
