extraction.body: Jordanian authorities said on Monday that they will block the Telegram social media app in the kingdom over national security concerns.Jordanian Telegram users reported disruptions on Monday, according to Jordanian news outlet Roya News. Shortly after, Jordan's Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced it had blocked the messaging app nationwide.Telegram, a Dubai-based cloud messaging app for mobile and desktop, describes itself on its website as focused on security and speed. It supports end-to-end encrypted chats with self-destruct timers for sensitive messages.Jordan cites crime, extremismThe PSD said the move was meant to stop the platform from being used for cybercrime, threats, extortion, and the spread of illegal content, including extremist material, according to the Jordanian state news agency Petra.The decision comes after a rare deadly church attack last month killed nine people and prompted airstrikes on neighboring Syria that Jordan said killed 20 Islamic State terrorists. On November 5, Jordan said one security officer had been killed and another wounded in what it called a terrorist stabbing attack in Amman.Blocking Telegram is one of several measures aimed specifically at combating Islamist terrorism, Prof. Ronen Yitzhak, an expert on Jordan and head of Bar-Ilan University's Department of Multidisciplinary Studies in the Humanities, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.Jordan has intensified its war on terror, Yitzhak said, not only through counterterrorism operations, such as strikes on Islamic State strongholds in southern Syria, but also by taking the fight to social media. The move is also meant to give Jordanian citizens a renewed sense of security, he added.Barak Gonen, a cybersecurity expert and lecturer at the Jerusalem College of Technology, was more skeptical. Blocking Telegram because it was presumably used to facilitate terrorist attacks is “equivalent [to] stopping all the train transportation in the country because some terrorists are known to be on a train,” he told the Post on Monday.The move is legitimate, Gonen said, but “very extreme.”“I certainly do hope that in [Israel, the Shin Bet] has the capabilities of stopping the specific train without stopping all of the train activity in the country,” he said.Directorate encourages parents to monitor children's online activityBlocking the Telegram app aligns with Jordan's existing legislation to "protect society from the risks associated with the misuse of digital platforms," the PSD claimed, according to Petra.The directorate also urged citizens to use social media with caution, avoid interacting with suspicious accounts or unknown users, and report illegal activity. It called on parents to monitor their children's internet use, use parental controls on internet-connected devices, and “encourage safe and responsible use of technology.”Telegram did not immediately respond to The Jerusalem Post's request for comment. However, the company's automatic reply noted that “Telegram is committed to protecting user privacy and human rights such as freedom of speech and assembly.”Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, is regarded as a relatively stable state in the Middle East. Its security services have foiled plots by Islamist terrorists in the past, including suspected Islamic State supporters.Over the years, Islamic State militants have used the mobile messaging service, created by Pavel Durov, who is in exile from Russia, to issue statements.Durov faces investigations in several countries. In July, Russia said it had ​charged him with facilitating terrorist activity, alleging that his app was being used by ‌Ukrainian spies to organize attacks inside Russia.Durov denies wrongdoing and says Telegram has exceeded its obligations to moderate content and cooperate with authorities to fight crime. Iraq also moves to block TelegramLater on Monday, Iraq's Communications and Media Commission (CMC) announced that Telegram would be blocked across the country, “due to the company's failure to comply with the applicable legal and regulatory requirements.”The move is meant to push the company to review Iraqi content on the app, prevent violations, and cooperate with the commission, the CMC said, as part of wider efforts to curb the use of social media to spread extremism, incite sedition, violence, and hatred, commit cybercrime, and threaten national security.According to the CMC, Telegram did not take adequate action to combat the dissemination of content that violates Iraqi law. The commission gave Telegram a 30-day grace period to rectify the situation, although it did not specify what would happen if Telegram failed to do so.The ban comes six months after the commission lifted a week-long ban on the messaging app in May, after the company complied with the regulator's rules, according to Kurdistan Region-based news channel Rudaw Media Network. The commission had cited national security concerns then as well.The app has found a range of uses in Iraq, including by channels affiliated with pro-Iran armed groups, some of which decried Monday's decision, Rudaw reported.It also comes nearly a month after Iraq's Communications Ministry banned the navigation app Waze, citing the presence of the company's data centers in Israel, Rudaw reported.Reuters contributed to this report.

extraction.body: Calls for governments to recognise sexual exploitation of children as preventable public health emergency Calls for governments to recognise sexual exploitation of children as preventable public health emergency Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found. A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images. The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children . Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation. The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe. Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online. “But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.” A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online , with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025. IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500. The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF. Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year. It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting. Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”. The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada. Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years. “While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.” Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk. “We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature. But there is nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse. We have the knowledge and tools to make a difference. “We are calling on governments to recognise this as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action. With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.”

AI-generated child sexual abuse imagery has escalated by more than 8,400 per cent over a two-year timeframe, according to international research. The global investigation revealed that documented cases worldwide grew by upwards of 395,300 between 2023 and 2025. Academics also calculated that over 300 million children across the globe suffer at least one instance of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse annually. Furthermore, approximately one in four young people can expect to face some form of online abuse prior to turning 18. The statistics were compiled as part of a major international project involving Scottish experts from the Childlight Global Child Safety Institute , based at the University of Edinburgh . Childlight highlighted that referrals of AI-generated abuse material provided by technology firms to the US-based National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children surged from approximately 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The material includes “ deepfakes ”, which are created using so-called “nudify apps”, where the face of a real child can be digitally placed onto sexually explicit images in a realistic manner within seconds. Although the images may be fake, researchers said the harm to children is very real, with images sometimes used to blackmail children, demanding money or more images. Researchers said the problem affects ordinary people as well as high-profile celebrities. However, the study cautioned that changes in detection and reporting may have contributed to the dramatic increase. Professor Debi Fry, Childlight’s global director of data at Edinburgh University, said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. “These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.” She added: “While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.” Childlight’s new international study also warned that serious gaps in government data are hampering prevention efforts to protect children. Of 103 countries and areas examined across the three regions, the group said only 22 had representative survey data covering both offline and technology-facilitated abuse. According to Childlight, children with disabilities, Indigenous children, migrants, those in humanitarian settings, very young children and children abused within their families are particularly underrepresented. In response, Childlight is urging governments to treat sexual exploitation and abuse as a preventable public health issue, invest in reliable and consistent measurement, and use evidence to strengthen protection, support survivors and prevent harm before it occurs. The institute is also calling for stronger technology-sector accountability, laws that keep pace with emerging threats and prevention efforts beginning earlier in childhood. Childlight chief executive Paul Stanfield said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk. “What remains invisible risks remaining unaddressed. We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature.” Mr Stanfield, there is “nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse”. He added: “With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.” Despite the challenges, the report highlighted encouraging progress, with several countries strengthening online safety legislation, improving detection and focusing more on prevention. With better intelligence, coordinated action and sustained investment, researchers said governments have an opportunity to protect hundreds of millions of children and help create a safer future. The findings are contained in the group’s 2026 Into the Light Index, which was unveiled at a global summit involving representatives from more than 100 governments on ending violence against children on Monday.

Mr Stanfield, there is “nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse”.

(Bloomberg) -- Bitcoin options traders are bracing for further losses after last week's bruising selloff, as a tougher interest-rate outlook and a risk-off mood deepen the gloom around the cryptocurrency. 'I'm a Piece of Sh--': Jensen Huang's Last Hours as Nvidia CEO Huang Discusses Comeback as Nvidia Chief With Allies, Report Says Thousands of US Flights Disrupted as Nationwide Halt Extends Nvidia Feels the Heat on CEO Search as Bessent Calls for Shakeup VC Firm Run by Madonna's Manager Has $7 Billion Anthropic Stake The largest concentration of put open interest on Deribit stood at the $60,000 strike across all expiries on Monday, about 8% below Bitcoin's current price of around $65,000. Puts, which give holders the right to sell at a predetermined price, are often used as protection when further drops are expected. The positioning follows an especially sharp drop in Bitcoin last week, which saw the largest digital asset fall by 12%. It hit a four-month low of nearly $62,000 over the weekend before clawing back some of those losses. In the options market, traders remain wary. "Market participants were looking to hedge short-term downside risk via options in very thin liquidity," said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. During the selloff, a gauge comparing the pricing of puts and calls expiring Friday reached 25 points in favor of puts, according to Mauron. That showed strong demand for protection against a further drop. "The $60,000 level has been established as a strong support, holding up twice this year as well as throughout 2024," Mauron said. A decisive break below that level could inflict serious pain on the market, she added, with no obvious support before $40,000. Bitcoin briefly fell through $60,000 on July 1, hitting a low of $57,742 for the year, but it has traded above that level since July 2. The token's latest swoon has come as several of the forces that once helped push it higher have reversed. Investors have pulled almost $3 billion from US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds since the $6 billion Binance hack on Oct. 29, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The outflows have removed a source of demand that had helped underpin the cryptocurrency. At the same time, the outlook for US interest rates has turned more negative. Traders have added to bets on further Federal Reserve rate increases in 2027 and have begun assigning a small probability to a half-percentage-point increase in December after inflation again topped forecasts. Crypto has also been swept up in a broader retreat from risk assets, fueled by turmoil around the artificial-intelligence trade. "The problem is that Bitcoin is competing for attention in a crowded macro environment," said Robin Singh, chief executive officer of Koinly. "Between the Nvidia controversy, growing economic uncertainty and geopolitical tensions, investors have plenty of other things to worry about." That leaves Bitcoin short of an obvious catalyst to draw buyers back in, according to Singh, who said the cryptocurrency could struggle to rebuild momentum. To be sure, Jeff Ko, chief analyst at ViaBTC, said Bitcoin may be nearing a turning point. "Much of the recent decline presumably reflects capital rotating into Anthropic's IPO, as investors sold liquid assets to fund their allocations," he said, adding the token saw a similar selloff ahead of the SpaceX IPO and then rebounded quickly. "The drop to $62,000 over the weekend also flushed out a large share of leveraged speculative positions," Ko said. "I think that gives a healthier base for a recovery." For now, technical indicators offer little comfort. The latest decline brought Bitcoin back below its 200-day and 200-week moving averages — levels seen as key long-term indicators. That "paints a bearish picture in the short term," according to Pratik Kala, a portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto. This leaves options traders focused on a support level that has already shown resilience twice this year, with hopes that it may pull off a third rebound.

sources.title: Bitcoin's Biggest Options Wager Flips to a $60,000 Put as Traders Hedge a Slide - BigGo Finance
passages: Bitcoin's most crowded derivatives position is no longer a bet on a moonshot.
After a sharp slide, the largest single options wager on Deribit is now a put at the $60,000 strike, carrying roughly $900 million in notional open interest, according to CoinDesk.
The backdrop matters for how the positioning should be read.
Bitcoin spent much of the year climbing from roughly $64,000 to more than $85,000 during an August-September surge that concentrated open interest in upside calls.
The subsequent retreat has forced traders to reprice risk, and the options market is now split between those defending against a deeper drop and those who simply cashed out of bullish wagers.
The shift caps a turbulent stretch for the largest cryptocurrency.
Bitcoin fell as far as the low $60,000s before recovering to trade around $64,000, a bounce that suggests buyers are stepping in at lower levels but has yet to produce a convincing breakout.
For investors, the practical signal is less about a forecast of $60,000 than about where protection is concentrated.
A large put strike can act as a magnet for hedging flows and amplify moves as expiry approaches, but it does not by itself dictate spot prices.
The contract pays off if bitcoin trades below $60,000, making it a form of insurance against further losses.
Nicolas Quatravaux, head of EMEA at Paradigm, a crypto derivatives liquidity network, cautioned that the headline number says more about the past than the present.
"OI is a stock, not a flow; it shows what's been built up over months, not what people are doing today," he said.
Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search Top Stories, so you get the broadest, most up-to-the-minute, and most comprehensive global financial news first.
The size is tracking spot and sitting just above $60,000 rather than on it, Quatravaux said, with two-way trading and put spreads such as 60/64 changing hands in smaller clips around that level.
Other flows point to more nuanced positioning.

SignalPlus flagged interest in multi-legged structures over the weekend, including a put ratio backspread in which a market participant bought 750 BTC of $68,000 puts and sold 500 BTC of $72,000 puts, all expiring Nov.
That trade profits from a sharp decline but not from a decline alone, with maximum loss at expiry near $68,000 and break-even prices around $62,380 and $70,650.
Put diagonal spreads, designed to profit from a controlled or gradual decline into mid-to-late November, also drew interest.

After a sharp slide, the largest single options wager on Deribit is now a put at the $60,000 strike, carrying roughly $900 million in notional open interest, according to CoinDesk. The contract pays off if bitcoin trades below $60,000, making it a form of insurance against further losses. It displaced the $100,000 call, which had held the top spot through the late-summer rally and now sits second with about $867 million in open interest. The shift caps a turbulent stretch for the largest cryptocurrency. Bitcoin fell as far as the low $60,000s before recovering to trade around $64,000, a bounce that suggests buyers are stepping in at lower levels but has yet to produce a convincing breakout. The $64,000 zone is now the first technical hurdle on the upside; a failure there would put the $62,000 support back in play, with a break below opening the door to $60,000. Note: One Deribit contract represents one bitcoin. Nicolas Quatravaux, head of EMEA at Paradigm, a crypto derivatives liquidity network, cautioned that the headline number says more about the past than the present. The $60,000 put has been the go-to protection strike all year, he told CoinDesk, with heavy buying on Paradigm whenever the market wobbled in February, March and again in June. "OI is a stock, not a flow; it shows what's been built up over months, not what people are doing today," he said. The call's demotion, meanwhile, reflects position unwinding rather than a rush into bearish bets. Traders bought more than 12,000 BTC of $100,000 calls on Paradigm in September during the squeeze and sold back roughly 6,700 BTC of them in October, according to Quatravaux. "So the 100k call didn't lose the top spot because everyone rushed into puts; it's more that the upside bets got taken off," he said. Recent put activity has been dominated by a single large player rolling a sizable position to progressively lower strikes as spot price declined, from $74,000 in late October through $72,000, $68,000, $65,000 and $63,000 by the end of November, amounting to more than $1 billion of put blocks on Paradigm in two days. The size is tracking spot and sitting just above $60,000 rather than on it, Quatravaux said, with two-way trading and put spreads such as 60/64 changing hands in smaller clips around that level. Other flows point to more nuanced positioning. SignalPlus flagged interest in multi-legged structures over the weekend, including a put ratio backspread in which a market participant bought 750 BTC of $68,000 puts and sold 500 BTC of $72,000 puts, all expiring Nov. 27. That trade profits from a sharp decline but not from a decline alone, with maximum loss at expiry near $68,000 and break-even prices around $62,380 and $70,650. Put diagonal spreads, designed to profit from a controlled or gradual decline into mid-to-late November, also drew interest. The hedging impulse showed up in volatility pricing as well. Volmex's bitcoin 30-day implied volatility index, BVIV, jumped to 57.13 points on Sunday, its highest since June, before retreating to 44 as the initial panic faded. Cole Garner, founder of Volmex, pointed to a run of negative headlines, including exchange security worries, AI-related market uncertainty and a tougher regulatory outlook, as the driver of the jitters. The backdrop matters for how the positioning should be read. Bitcoin spent much of the year climbing from roughly $64,000 to more than $85,000 during an August-September surge that concentrated open interest in upside calls. The subsequent retreat has forced traders to reprice risk, and the options market is now split between those defending against a deeper drop and those who simply cashed out of bullish wagers. For investors, the practical signal is less about a forecast of $60,000 than about where protection is concentrated. A large put strike can act as a magnet for hedging flows and amplify moves as expiry approaches, but it does not by itself dictate spot prices. What matters over the coming sessions is whether bitcoin can hold above $64,000 and keep the $62,000 support intact; a decisive break lower would test the conviction of the traders who have spent months building positions around the $60,000 level. The positioning matters because hedges can shape how the price moves as it nears key levels. Bitcoin has struggled to hold any bounce this month. Traders now want to know whether buyers can defend the first floor or whether put holders will collect.
Demand has grown for contracts that pay out if the price falls toward $60,000. No single fund or trader stands behind the move. The flow looks like broad hedging across the market.

The week explains the caution. Bitcoin lost about 14% over seven days, and each bounce faded quickly. Buyers who stepped in early were left holding losses. Many holders now prefer insurance over fresh bets on a rebound.

That shift matters for how the market trades. Downside protection has become the crowded position, and crowded positions shape behavior. Traders who sold or bought those puts will adjust their hedges as the price nears the strike.
The round number now works as a target for bears and a test of nerve for everyone else.

Bitcoin traded near $64,000 at last check, and the broader chart looks heavy. The price sits under both of the moving averages that traders use to judge the long trend. A moving average smooths out daily swings to show the typical price over a set period.

The 50-day average stands near $77,000. The 200-day average sits just below it. Both lines hover well above the current price. They now act as ceilings, levels where past buyers may sell to break even.

The shorter average has slipped toward the longer one, which shows that recent weeks were weaker than the past several months. Sellers have controlled the trend for a while, and each rally has stalled long before reaching those lines.

The monthly picture adds to the strain. Bitcoin fell about 21% over the past 30 days. That decline leaves the price pinned near the bottom of its range for the month, with little cushion from recent lows.
A recovery would be hard. Bitcoin would need to climb roughly $12,000 just to touch the 200-day line. A move that size would take sustained buying, and buyers have shown little of it so far.

RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, reads about 22 on the daily chart. Anything below 30 counts as oversold. That means the selling has run far and fast, and readings this low often come before a relief bounce.

Other signals still favor the bears. The MACD, a tool that tracks shifts in momentum, remains below its signal line, so momentum is still pointing down. Trend strength readings confirm a real trend, and sellers are leading it.

Recent trading offered a small hint of relief. Bitcoin slipped only about 1% over the past day, a far gentler pace than earlier in the week. That suggests the pressure may be easing. It does not yet show buyers taking control.

The first floor sits near $62,000, just below the current price. Buyers defended this area recently, so it is the first real test for the bears. A daily close beneath it would show that demand has thinned out.

If that floor gives way, the next support waits near $59,000. That level sits just under the options target. A slide there would hand the put buyers their payout and could trigger more hedging as dealers adjust.

The bias stays bearish until Bitcoin climbs back above its long averages. Sellers still drive the trend, and the put buyers' target sits only a short drop away.
Late bears face a real risk, though. Deeply oversold markets can snap higher without warning. A sharp short squeeze would punish traders who piled into downside bets near the lows.

passages: Bitcoin's most crowded derivatives position is no longer a bet on a moonshot.
After a sharp slide, the largest single options wager on Deribit is now a put at the $60,000 strike, carrying roughly $900 million in notional open interest, according to CoinDesk.
The backdrop matters for how the positioning should be read.
Bitcoin spent much of the year climbing from roughly $64,000 to more than $85,000 during an August-September surge that concentrated open interest in upside calls.
The subsequent retreat has forced traders to reprice risk, and the options market is now split between those defending against a deeper drop and those who simply cashed out of bullish wagers.
The shift caps a turbulent stretch for the largest cryptocurrency.
Bitcoin fell as far as the low $60,000s before recovering to trade around $64,000, a bounce that suggests buyers are stepping in at lower levels but has yet to produce a convincing breakout.
For investors, the practical signal is less about a forecast of $60,000 than about where protection is concentrated.
A large put strike can act as a magnet for hedging flows and amplify moves as expiry approaches, but it does not by itself dictate spot prices.
The contract pays off if bitcoin trades below $60,000, making it a form of insurance against further losses.
Nicolas Quatravaux, head of EMEA at Paradigm, a crypto derivatives liquidity network, cautioned that the headline number says more about the past than the present.
"OI is a stock, not a flow; it shows what's been built up over months, not what people are doing today," he said.

The size is tracking spot and sitting just above $60,000 rather than on it, Quatravaux said, with two-way trading and put spreads such as 60/64 changing hands in smaller clips around that level.
Other flows point to more nuanced positioning.

That trade profits from a sharp decline but not from a decline alone, with maximum loss at expiry near $68,000 and break-even prices around $62,380 and $70,650.
Put diagonal spreads, designed to profit from a controlled or gradual decline into mid-to-late November, also drew interest.

The contract pays off if bitcoin trades below $60,000, making it a form of insurance against further losses. It displaced the $100,000 call, which had held the top spot through the late-summer rally and now sits second with about $867 million in open interest. The shift caps a turbulent stretch for the largest cryptocurrency. Bitcoin fell as far as the low $60,000s before recovering to trade around $64,000, a bounce that suggests buyers are stepping in at lower levels but has yet to produce a convincing breakout. The $64,000 zone is now the first technical hurdle on the upside; a failure there would put the $62,000 support back in play, with a break below opening the door to $60,000. Note: One Deribit contract represents one bitcoin. Nicolas Quatravaux, head of EMEA at Paradigm, a crypto derivatives liquidity network, cautioned that the headline number says more about the past than the present. The $60,000 put has been the go-to protection strike all year, he told CoinDesk, with heavy buying on Paradigm whenever the market wobbled in February, March and again in June. "OI is a stock, not a flow; it shows what's been built up over months, not what people are doing today," he said. The call's demotion, meanwhile, reflects position unwinding rather than a rush into bearish bets. Traders bought more than 12,000 BTC of $100,000 calls on Paradigm in September during the squeeze and sold back roughly 6,700 BTC of them in October, according to Quatravaux. "So the 100k call didn't lose the top spot because everyone rushed into puts; it's more that the upside bets got taken off," he said. Recent put activity has been dominated by a single large player rolling a sizable position to progressively lower strikes as spot price declined, from $74,000 in late October through $72,000, $68,000, $65,000 and $63,000 by the end of November, amounting to more than $1 billion of put blocks on Paradigm in two days. The size is tracking spot and sitting just above $60,000 rather than on it, Quatravaux said, with two-way trading and put spreads such as 60/64 changing hands in smaller clips around that level. Other flows point to more nuanced positioning. That trade profits from a sharp decline but not from a decline alone, with maximum loss at expiry near $68,000 and break-even prices around $62,380 and $70,650. Put diagonal spreads, designed to profit from a controlled or gradual decline into mid-to-late November, also drew interest. The hedging impulse showed up in volatility pricing as well. Volmex's bitcoin 30-day implied volatility index, BVIV, jumped to 57.13 points on Sunday, its highest since June, before retreating to 44 as the initial panic faded. For investors, the practical signal is less about a forecast of $60,000 than about where protection is concentrated. A large put strike can act as a magnet for hedging flows and amplify moves as expiry approaches, but it does not by itself dictate spot prices. What matters over the coming sessions is whether bitcoin can hold above $64,000 and keep the $62,000 support intact; a decisive break lower would test the conviction of the traders who have spent months building positions around the $60,000 level. Bitcoin would need to climb roughly $12,000 just to touch the 200-day line. A move that size would take sustained buying, and buyers have shown little of it so far. RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, reads about 22 on the daily chart. Anything below 30 counts as oversold. That means the selling has run far and fast, and readings this low often come before a relief bounce. An oversold reading alone is a weak reason to buy. The first floor sits near $62,000, just below the current price. Buyers defended this area recently, so it is the first real test for the bears. A daily close beneath it would show that demand has thinned out.

If that floor gives way, the next support waits near $59,000. That level sits just under the options target. A slide there would hand the put buyers their payout and could trigger more hedging as dealers adjust.

Overhead, the first resistance stands near $75,000, close to both long averages. Bitcoin would need to reclaim that zone to break the bearish case. A move back above it would leave the downside contracts looking like expensive insurance.
The second ceiling sits near $80,000. A climb through that level would confirm a full trend reversal. Sellers would lose control, and the options crowd would need a new plan.
The next three days should show whether the selloff runs its course or reaches the bears' target.
The bias stays bearish until Bitcoin climbs back above its long averages. Sellers still drive the trend, and the put buyers' target sits only a short drop away.
Late bears face a real risk, though. Deeply oversold markets can snap higher without warning. A sharp short squeeze would punish traders who piled into downside bets near the lows.

The move capped a sharp reversal from the $58,293 low Bitcoin touched on July 1. A softer-than-expected jobs report reshaped rate-hike expectations heading into the new week, helping Bitcoin’s price claw back. The rally traces back to Thursday’s US Nonfarm Payrolls report . The report showed the economy added just 57,000 jobs in June, far below forecasts. The miss lowered the odds of a near-term Federal Reserve rate hike, and Bitcoin had already gained ground on Warsh’s inflation risk comments earlier in the week. Lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar reduced the opportunity cost of holding Bitcoin, helping the asset recover from a bearish June. Spot Bitcoin ETFs added to the momentum. An ETF inflow reversal snapped a 10-day run of redemptions, though the funds are still working through June’s record outflows of $4.5 billion. A weekend of rising price action was capped by a spike towards $64,000. Image Source: BeInCrypto Traders lost over $450 million in short positions across the derivatives market as Bitcoin broke through $62,000. Bitcoin’s price reflected the broader squeeze dynamic, in which forced buybacks push the price into the next tranche of shorts. Ether rose roughly 4% on the day and about 10% over the week, while Solana added nearly 19%, the strongest gain among major tokens. Institutional flows have not fully confirmed the move, with ETFs still recovering from their worst month on record. Whether the squeeze becomes a durable trend remains an open question. Forced short-covering tends to produce fast price moves rather than sustained demand. The market now enters the third quarter with thinner liquidity, a dynamic that could cut in either direction. Traders lost over $450 million in short positions across the derivatives market as Bitcoin broke through $62,000. Bitcoin’s price reflected the broader squeeze dynamic, in which forced buybacks push the price into the next tranche of shorts.

Ether rose roughly 4% on the day and about 10% over the week, while Solana added nearly 19%, the strongest gain among major tokens. Institutional flows have not fully confirmed the move, with ETFs still recovering from their worst month on record.

Whether the squeeze becomes a durable trend remains an open question. Forced short-covering tends to produce fast price moves rather than sustained demand. The market now enters the third quarter with thinner liquidity, a dynamic that could cut in either direction.

The slide has been punishing for leveraged traders. About $2 billion of crypto positions were liquidated over a 24-hour period during the weekend, the vast majority of them long bets. Bitcoin is now down 17% in November and has posted six straight weekly losses. Stock futures offered little help on Monday. Contracts on the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.5% and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.7%, while Nvidia fell 3% in premarket trading. Investors weighed a Financial Times report that former CEO Jensen Huang and his allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him, a week after his resignation sent bitcoin below $72,000 . Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, and options markets imply an earnings-day move of about 7% in either direction, Pepperstone’s Chris Weston told Reuters. Bitcoin has traded in step with chip stocks for much of the past week, so a weak report could add to the pressure. Rates remain the other weight on the bitcoin price. Traders fully price a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December meeting, with odds of a half-point move near 8%, CME FedWatch data show. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.12% on Monday after jumping 29 basis points last week, and higher yields have lifted the dollar to its strongest level since April 2025. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks in San Francisco later Monday, and minutes from the last Fed meeting are due Wednesday. Bitcoin-linked stocks fell with the coin. Strategy (MSTR) was down 8% in premarket trading and Strive (ASST) fell 9%. Strategy is also facing index-fund selling after MSCI removed it from its USA index , forcing index funds to sell by Nov. 30. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed another $185 million on Friday, their seventh straight day of outflows, bringing losses since Nov. 5 to about $1.91 billion. That run follows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bleeding $2 billion over nine straight sessions. Analysts are now focused on the $60,000 level, which marked the lows of February and June. John Roque, technical strategist at 22V Research, said bitcoin is close to completing a head-and-shoulders top. “Bitcoin has not broken below its neckline at 60,000,” he wrote in a note Saturday, adding that such a breach “would then imply risk to $38,000.” Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co., wrote that bitcoin “NEEDS to hold the $60k level,” warning that “any material break below that level would be quite bearish.” A gauge of bitcoin’s 30-day implied volatility climbed to 49.75 over the weekend, its highest since June. With Nvidia’s report, Fed speakers and the Fed minutes all due in the next three days, the bitcoin price faces a busy week. A move back above $66,000 would recover Sunday’s bounce high, while a break below the weekend low near $62,000 would put the $60,000 floor in play. At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $64,100. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. Binance Research said the decline extended BTC's losses to 15.6% over 11 days, which is its sharpest comparable selloff since June. The selling pressure has pushed Bitcoin into a price region that on-chain analytics firm Glassnode had identified as particularly vulnerable. Bitcoin's latest downturn has exposed a striking disparity in selling pressure between dollar-denominated trading venues and Binance , suggesting risk aversion is particularly pronounced in USD markets. Between Nov. 11 and Nov. 14, aggressive selling exceeded buying by 7,438 BTC on a major dollar-based spot exchange, compared with 2,707 BTC on Binance, according to Binance Research . The reported selling imbalance on the unnamed USD venue was about 2.75 times Binance’s. The pressure has also coincided with substantial withdrawals from US-listed investment products. US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded nearly $2 billion in net outflows across seven consecutive sessions from Nov. 5 through Nov. 13, according to Farside Investors . Binance Research linked the simultaneous pressures to mounting uncertainty over interest rates, dollar liquidity and the sustainability of the artificial intelligence investment boom. The concerns have coincided with upheaval at Nvidia, where Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as chief executive on Nov. 12, leaving longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO as investors scrutinize the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending ahead of Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. However, Strive CEO Matt Cole believes Bitcoin's current weakness resembles the conditions surrounding SpaceX's record-breaking public offering earlier this year. Cole observed that Bitcoin declined 19% over the 50 days before SpaceX's June 12 listing , closely resembling the 18% decline ahead of Anthropic's planned IPO when he made the comparison on Nov. 13. Anthropic’s proposed offering could total about $64 billion at the top of its indicated price range, including shares sold by existing holders. The earlier episode also suggests that additional losses could precede any sustained recovery. extraction.body: Bitcoin ( BTC ) spiked to nearly $64,000 in the early hours of July 6, reaching $63,900 on CoinGecko, extending a weekend rally that liquidated hundreds of millions of dollars in short positions. The move capped a sharp reversal from the $58,293 low Bitcoin touched on July 1. A softer-than-expected jobs report reshaped rate-hike expectations heading into the new week, helping Bitcoin’s price claw back. The rally traces back to Thursday’s US Nonfarm Payrolls report . The report showed the economy added just 57,000 jobs in June, far below forecasts. The miss lowered the odds of a near-term Federal Reserve rate hike, and Bitcoin had already gained ground on Warsh’s inflation risk comments earlier in the week. Lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar reduced the opportunity cost of holding Bitcoin, helping the asset recover from a bearish June. Spot Bitcoin ETFs added to the momentum. An ETF inflow reversal snapped a 10-day run of redemptions, though the funds are still working through June’s record outflows of $4.5 billion. A weekend of rising price action was capped by a spike towards $64,000. Image Source: BeInCrypto Traders lost over $450 million in short positions across the derivatives market as Bitcoin broke through $62,000. Bitcoin’s price reflected the broader squeeze dynamic, in which forced buybacks push the price into the next tranche of shorts. Ether rose roughly 4% on the day and about 10% over the week, while Solana added nearly 19%, the strongest gain among major tokens. Institutional flows have not fully confirmed the move, with ETFs still recovering from their worst month on record. Whether the squeeze becomes a durable trend remains an open question. Forced short-covering tends to produce fast price moves rather than sustained demand. The market now enters the third quarter with thinner liquidity, a dynamic that could cut in either direction. The selling that broke Friday’s low on Saturday morning did not stop there. Bitcoin slipped under $64,000 Saturday afternoon and dropped below $62,000 in the 8 p.m. ET hour on some exchanges, its lowest level since July 14. It bounced back above $64,800 within the hour and reached about $66,100 early Sunday before sellers returned. The bitcoin price has spent most of the past day between $64,000 and $65,000. The slide has been punishing for leveraged traders. About $2 billion of crypto positions were liquidated over a 24-hour period during the weekend, the vast majority of them long bets. Bitcoin is now down 17% in November and has posted six straight weekly losses. Stock futures offered little help on Monday. Contracts on the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.5% and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.7%, while Nvidia fell 3% in premarket trading. Investors weighed a Financial Times report that former CEO Jensen Huang and his allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him, a week after his resignation sent bitcoin below $72,000 . Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, and options markets imply an earnings-day move of about 7% in either direction, Pepperstone’s Chris Weston told Reuters. Bitcoin has traded in step with chip stocks for much of the past week, so a weak report could add to the pressure. Rates remain the other weight on the bitcoin price. Traders fully price a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December meeting, with odds of a half-point move near 8%, CME FedWatch data show. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.12% on Monday after jumping 29 basis points last week, and higher yields have lifted the dollar to its strongest level since April 2025. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks in San Francisco later Monday, and minutes from the last Fed meeting are due Wednesday. Bitcoin-linked stocks fell with the coin. Strategy (MSTR) was down 8% in premarket trading and Strive (ASST) fell 9%. Strategy is also facing index-fund selling after MSCI removed it from its USA index , forcing index funds to sell by Nov. 30. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed another $185 million on Friday, their seventh straight day of outflows, bringing losses since Nov. 5 to about $1.91 billion. That run follows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bleeding $2 billion over nine straight sessions. Analysts are now focused on the $60,000 level, which marked the lows of February and June. John Roque, technical strategist at 22V Research, said bitcoin is close to completing a head-and-shoulders top. “Bitcoin has not broken below its neckline at 60,000,” he wrote in a note Saturday, adding that such a breach “would then imply risk to $38,000.” Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co., wrote that bitcoin “NEEDS to hold the $60k level,” warning that “any material break below that level would be quite bearish.” A gauge of bitcoin’s 30-day implied volatility climbed to 49.75 over the weekend, its highest since June. With Nvidia’s report, Fed speakers and the Fed minutes all due in the next three days, the bitcoin price faces a busy week. A move back above $66,000 would recover Sunday’s bounce high, while a break below the weekend low near $62,000 would put the $60,000 floor in play. At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $64,100. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. The slide has been punishing for leveraged traders. About $2 billion of crypto positions were liquidated over a 24-hour period during the weekend, the vast majority of them long bets. Bitcoin is now down 17% in November and has posted six straight weekly losses.

Stock futures offered little help on Monday. Contracts on the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.5% and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.7%, while Nvidia fell 3% in premarket trading. Investors weighed a Financial Times report that former CEO Jensen Huang and his allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him, a week after his resignation sent bitcoin below $72,000 .

Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, and options markets imply an earnings-day move of about 7% in either direction, Pepperstone’s Chris Weston told Reuters. Bitcoin has traded in step with chip stocks for much of the past week, so a weak report could add to the pressure.

Rates remain the other weight on the bitcoin price. Traders fully price a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December meeting, with odds of a half-point move near 8%, CME FedWatch data show. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.12% on Monday after jumping 29 basis points last week, and higher yields have lifted the dollar to its strongest level since April 2025. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks in San Francisco later Monday, and minutes from the last Fed meeting are due Wednesday.

Bitcoin-linked stocks fell with the coin. Strategy (MSTR) was down 8% in premarket trading and Strive (ASST) fell 9%. Strategy is also facing index-fund selling after MSCI removed it from its USA index , forcing index funds to sell by Nov. 30.

Spot bitcoin ETFs shed another $185 million on Friday, their seventh straight day of outflows, bringing losses since Nov. 5 to about $1.91 billion. That run follows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bleeding $2 billion over nine straight sessions.

Analysts are now focused on the $60,000 level, which marked the lows of February and June. John Roque, technical strategist at 22V Research, said bitcoin is close to completing a head-and-shoulders top. “Bitcoin has not broken below its neckline at 60,000,” he wrote in a note Saturday, adding that such a breach “would then imply risk to $38,000.”

Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co., wrote that bitcoin “NEEDS to hold the $60k level,” warning that “any material break below that level would be quite bearish.” A gauge of bitcoin’s 30-day implied volatility climbed to 49.75 over the weekend, its highest since June.

With Nvidia’s report, Fed speakers and the Fed minutes all due in the next three days, the bitcoin price faces a busy week. A move back above $66,000 would recover Sunday’s bounce high, while a break below the weekend low near $62,000 would put the $60,000 floor in play.
At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $64,100.

16, citing the platform's use to facilitate cybercrime, extremism and activities that threaten national security [1] .

The directorate said Telegram had provided "spaces for the spread of extremism and radicalism" and for crimes including threats, blackmail and the circulation of illegal content, and that the block was consistent with existing law [1] [2] .
Telegram users in Jordan reported widespread disruptions before the announcement, Roya News reported [1] .

Telegram, founded by Pavel Durov and based in Dubai, did not respond to The Jerusalem Post's request for comment; an automatic reply said the company "is committed to protecting user privacy and human rights such as freedom of speech and assembly" [2] .
Islamic State militants have used the app to issue statements over the years, and Russia said in July that it had charged Durov with facilitating terrorist activity, which he denies [2] .
Vietnam ordered telecom providers to block Telegram in May 2025, saying the company had not cooperated with criminal investigations; Telegram said it was surprised by the move [4] .
The statement did not name specific incidents.
5, Jordan said one security officer was killed and another wounded in what it called a terrorist stabbing attack in Amman [3] .

passages: LeoLabs has acquired FishEye Software as a wholly owned subsidiary, the company announced in a release dated November 16, 2026, to accelerate delivery of next-generation radars for missile warning and tracking.
FishEye is an engineering-services company specializing in mission-critical U.S. government defense systems.
It brings nearly 30 years of experience in systems engineering, software development and field testing for government-owned-and-operated radars supporting space domain awareness and missile defense.
The acquisition adds dozens of U.S. security-cleared systems engineers, software developers and radar experts , according to LeoLabs’ announcement summary.
For LeoLabs, the central execution task is to combine FishEye’s engineering resources with its manufacturing build-out and convert booked demand into operational radars on the timelines it has set.
That commitment is intended to expand U.S. radar manufacturing, strengthen the domestic supply chain and accelerate deployment of sensing infrastructure for national-security missions.
LeoLabs Seeker and Scout systems were already moving through its U.S. manufacturing line for delivery in 2027.

extraction.body: LeoLabs has acquired FishEye Software as a wholly owned subsidiary, the company announced in a release dated November 16, 2026, to accelerate delivery of next-generation radars for missile warning and tracking. Financial terms were not disclosed. LeoLabs funded the transaction with proceeds from a loan provided by Hercules Capital ( HTGC ) . FishEye is an engineering-services company specializing in mission-critical U.S. government defense systems. It brings nearly 30 years of experience in systems engineering, software development and field testing for government-owned-and-operated radars supporting space domain awareness and missile defense. The acquisition adds dozens of U.S. security-cleared systems engineers, software developers and radar experts , according to LeoLabs’ announcement summary. Chief Executive Tony Frazier made the software-integration rationale explicit: “FishEye brings decades of experience developing and integrating software for U.S. missile defense systems. That expertise will help us continue to adapt our proven radar technology for missile warning and tracking, and move those capabilities into operational use quickly.” The acquisition follows LeoLabs’ October 29, 2026 announcement of more than $100 million in 2026 bookings across U.S. and Allied customers. The company attributed the growth to accelerating demand for its next-generation radars supporting space superiority and missile defense. It is expanding capacity to build and field multiple radars concurrently. LeoLabs Seeker and Scout systems were already moving through its U.S. manufacturing line for delivery in 2027. The production ramp uses an established U.S. supply chain of contract manufacturers and component suppliers to increase output while maintaining delivery timelines. The additional capacity is intended to support both LeoLabs’ company-owned-and-operated radar network and sovereign systems delivered to government customers. Hiring is another part of that expansion. The October announcement described accelerated recruitment across radar and software engineering, manufacturing, systems integration and operations, with plans to nearly double the employee base by the end of 2026. FishEye adds an established engineering team to that broader build-out. The Hercules acquisition loan is separate from the up to $150 million conditional loan commitment LeoLabs announced on November 5, 2026, from the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital. That commitment is intended to expand U.S. radar manufacturing, strengthen the domestic supply chain and accelerate deployment of sensing infrastructure for national-security missions. The manufacturing expansion supported by the commitment includes completing two large-scale facilities by 2028 and adding dozens of radar systems to LeoLabs’ global network by 2030. It is also intended to expand deliveries of sovereign radars to U.S. and Allied government customers. The Office of Strategic Capital announcement identifies the transportable Scout-X as optimized for missile warning and tracking, the mission at the center of the FishEye acquisition. The deal therefore adds software, integration and field-test expertise to a wider production and financing effort. For LeoLabs, the central execution task is to combine FishEye’s engineering resources with its manufacturing build-out and convert booked demand into operational radars on the timelines it has set. Financial terms were not disclosed. LeoLabs funded the transaction with proceeds from a loan provided by Hercules Capital ( HTGC ) . FishEye is an engineering-services company specializing in mission-critical U.S. government defense systems. It brings nearly 30 years of experience in systems engineering, software development and field testing for government-owned-and-operated radars supporting space domain awareness and missile defense. The acquisition adds dozens of U.S. security-cleared systems engineers, software developers and radar experts , according to LeoLabs’ announcement summary. Chief Executive Tony Frazier made the software-integration rationale explicit: “FishEye brings decades of experience developing and integrating software for U.S. missile defense systems. That expertise will help us continue to adapt our proven radar technology for missile warning and tracking, and move those capabilities into operational use quickly.” The acquisition follows LeoLabs’ October 29, 2026 announcement of more than $100 million in 2026 bookings across U.S. and Allied customers. The company attributed the growth to accelerating demand for its next-generation radars supporting space superiority and missile defense. It is expanding capacity to build and field multiple radars concurrently. LeoLabs Seeker and Scout systems were already moving through its U.S. manufacturing line for delivery in 2027. The production ramp uses an established U.S. supply chain of contract manufacturers and component suppliers to increase output while maintaining delivery timelines. The additional capacity is intended to support both LeoLabs’ company-owned-and-operated radar network and sovereign systems delivered to government customers. Hiring is another part of that expansion. The October announcement described accelerated recruitment across radar and software engineering, manufacturing, systems integration and operations, with plans to nearly double the employee base by the end of 2026. FishEye adds an established engineering team to that broader build-out. The Hercules acquisition loan is separate from the up to $150 million conditional loan commitment LeoLabs announced on November 5, 2026, from the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital. That commitment is intended to expand U.S. radar manufacturing, strengthen the domestic supply chain and accelerate deployment of sensing infrastructure for national-security missions. The manufacturing expansion supported by the commitment includes completing two large-scale facilities by 2028 and adding dozens of radar systems to LeoLabs’ global network by 2030. It is also intended to expand deliveries of sovereign radars to U.S. and Allied government customers. The Office of Strategic Capital announcement identifies the transportable Scout-X as optimized for missile warning and tracking, the mission at the center of the FishEye acquisition. The deal therefore adds software, integration and field-test expertise to a wider production and financing effort. For LeoLabs, the central execution task is to combine FishEye’s engineering resources with its manufacturing build-out and convert booked demand into operational radars on the timelines it has set. passages: But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.” This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40).

But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.
That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.
The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support.
The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.
It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store.
You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad.
It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black.
The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks.

extraction.body: But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned. That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras. The Apple HomeView The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple. It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.) Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad. We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. The Apple Home Collection One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.” This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40). These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off. The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada. The HomePod Mini 2 Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis. Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black. One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing. It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface. You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer. Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10. The Apple TV 4K Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor. But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299. Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version. Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone. The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content. The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.

Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone.
The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content.
The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.

To say this is an important development would be a colossal understatement. The execution of this feature is the core of Apple’s game plan for the next few years, when it intends to release numerous products that leverage its iPhone app ecosystem to power Siri AI. Apple’s latest new product, the HomeView , is built around Siri AI. (It’s a light dash of Siri AI right now, but its links with content on individual iPhones show what the company is envisioning there.) The new Apple TV 4K has added microphones to make it an additional home access point for Siri AI. And there’s much more to come, as reported by Mark Gurman at Bloomberg : Apple needs software makers to begin preparing for what it hopes will be its flagship new product of 2027: smart glasses built around Siri AI, code-named N50. Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses, I’m told. The idea is to make those apps available through Siri, allowing users to get things done without grabbing their phones. Apple believes its large developer ecosystem could give it an advantage over Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, potentially providing countless third-party integrations when the glasses go on sale. Gurman expects the Siri-powered glasses (which are basically AirPods you wear on your face) to be released at WWDC , with a similar set of AirPods armed with AI-powered cameras set to debut later in the year. ( We’ll see .) These devices don’t make a lot of sense unless there’s a useful AI assistant behind them. Siri AI is not quite that yet—it’s more reliable and more useful than the old Siri was, but it’s not as good as it should be, and it’s sometimes very slow—but at least it’s promising. Still, just as the iPhone would be a lot less appealing if it only ran Apple-built apps, Siri AI is less appealing if it doesn’t have access to the functionality of the app ecosystem. Currently, Siri AI can use Spotlight to search content offered by third-party apps, but what it can’t do is learn about functionality offered by individual apps and command those apps to perform those functions in service of a larger request. That’s the goal of the Siri AI Developer Preview—and that sort of stuff is what’s going to make the HomeView (let alone glasses or AirPods paired with an iPhone) a more appealing product. If Apple can’t pull this off, well, it calls into question the trajectory of Apple’s entire future product strategy. extraction.body: But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned. That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras. The Apple HomeView The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple. It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.) Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad. We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. The Apple Home Collection One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.” This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40). These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off. The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada. The HomePod Mini 2 Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). passages: To say this is an important development would be a colossal understatement.
The execution of this feature is the core of Apple’s game plan for the next few years, when it intends to release numerous products that leverage its iPhone app ecosystem to power Siri AI.
Apple needs software makers to begin preparing for what it hopes will be its flagship new product of 2027: smart glasses built around Siri AI, code-named N50.
These devices don’t make a lot of sense unless there’s a useful AI assistant behind them.
Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses, I’m told.
The idea is to make those apps available through Siri, allowing users to get things done without grabbing their phones.

Apple believes its large developer ecosystem could give it an advantage over Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, potentially providing countless third-party integrations when the glasses go on sale.
